meta.blurb: Every lamp Wren Tallow lights hums to her, very softly. Then a kind stranger offers her a place at a school hidden inside a mountain. There the lamps are starting to fail, and the answer lies far below the Ninth Stair.
meta.bible: Wren Tallow: a twelve-year-old lamplighter's daughter from the village of Hollin Ford, who can hear the Hum inside things; patient, curious and brave. Alder Tallow: her father, the village lamplighter, gentle and proud. Master Ostrander Pike: the teacher of Listening, tall, thin and kind, with a lantern that burns without oil. Warden Isolde Marrow: head of the Academy, calm and serious, with a voice like a bell. Priya Anand: Wren's roommate from a faraway city, quick, brave and stubborn, who can calm frost. Tobias Kettle, called Tobe: Wren's roommate, a baker's son, nervous and clever with numbers. Cassian Vale: a proud student whose own hum is strong but harsh; nephew of Master Hale. Master Corvin Hale: the teacher of Stone, quiet and sad, who lost his daughter Elin. Elin Hale: his daughter, who went below the Ninth Stair long ago and was never seen again; only her Echo remains. Ibb: the old caretaker who knows the legends. Orrenfell: the mountain. The Academy Under the Mountain: the school inside Orrenfell, a cavern city of lamps, stone bridges and glowing moss. The Great Door: the cliff door that opens only to a listener's hum. The Hum: the faint song that lives in every stone, flame and living thing; students learn to hear it, hold it and lend it. The Heartstone: a vast crystal at the mountain's heart, whose hum lights the Academy. Ninth Stair: the lowest stair, forbidden to students; behind it lies the Hollow, the great chamber of the Heartstone. Sixth Gallery: the students' bedroom hall. Fifth Gallery: another hall where the lamps fail. Hall of Held Breath: the library of whispering books. Singing Falls: an underground waterfall. Lantern Night: the midwinter festival. The Long Note: the spring test of patience. Giving Back: the Academy's third rule and a new yearly tradition. The three rules: listen first; never go below the Ninth Stair; give back what you borrow. Silence jar: a glass bell jar Hale uses to hold stolen hum. Hollin Ford: Wren's village. Voice and tone: warm, curious and wondering, a mystery with a kind ending; no one is hurt and no one is evil, and the story is about listening, patience and giving back. ADDED FOR THE FULL BOOK: Dill Hobbs: a loud freckled village boy of Hollin Ford who calls Wren Wall-Ear, and in the end listens to her. Mags Fenner: an old neighbour who gives Wren a woollen scarf. Dumpling: Wren's round, slow, sure-footed mule. Sorrel: Pike's tall mule. Nan Crowe: the weathered old keeper of Crow's Rest, a stone hut on the mountain where travellers sleep; she keeps goats and knows the songs are thinning. Mistress Odalys Brook: the cheerful teacher of Echo, with grey curls and silver earrings. Velmara: Priya's faraway city of canals and bridges, twenty days away. Lowmarket: Tobe's home town, where his family keeps a bakery. Quiet Room: the round grey classroom where Listening and Tuning are taught. Hall of Lamps: the great round hall hung with a thousand lanterns. Skylight Shaft: the high chimney in the rock through which snow falls. Lamp tunnels: the narrow sooty passages behind the galleries. Eighth Gallery: a high balcony overlooking the great stair to the lower levels. The cloaked figure who draws hum into jars is Master Hale; he does it every ninth night from autumn to spring. Elin Hale went below the Ninth Stair alone thirty years ago, aged fifteen; her echo remains in the Heartstone. Brass bell: the small bell Pike gives the four friends to ring if they see anyone near the Ninth Stair. The Long Note is one hum held for a whole hour; every first year takes it in spring. Wren's hum lights lamps blue, Priya's silver, Tobe's gold. Tuning: the class where stones are tuned like strings. Wren's lantern: the small oil-free lantern Pike gives her at the end. Pike's lantern burns without oil. Warden Marrow returns early on the night of the bell. Giving Back is celebrated every spring by the whole school singing together in the great hall.
chapters: Three Beds in the Sixth Gallery
A Page in a Familiar Hand

beats.scene: Wren stands in a village lane at dusk, her ear against a glowing lamp
beats.summary: Wren, a lamplighter's daughter, can hear a faint hum inside every lamp in her village.

beats.scene: Wren climbs a ladder behind her father as he lights the lane's lamps
beats.summary: Each evening Wren follows her father Alder on his lamplighting round, and the lamps hum louder when she is near.

beats.scene: Wren rests her palm on the old stone wall beside the village well
beats.summary: Wren finds that stones hum too, much more slowly than flames, like something large and sleeping.

beats.scene: Village children point and laugh at Wren as she listens to the wall
beats.summary: The village children, led by Dill Hobbs, laugh at Wren and call her Wall-Ear.

beats.scene: Wren sits by the hearth as her father kneels beside her
beats.summary: Wren asks her father if she is strange; Alder says her gift is not strange, and tells her his grandmother heard lamps sing too.

beats.scene: Every lamp in the lane seems to lean toward a dark mountain
beats.summary: One autumn night all the village lamps seem to hum towards the north, where the great mountain Orrenfell stands.

beats.scene: Wren lies awake at her attic window, ear against the cold sill
beats.summary: Wren cannot sleep; the mountain's far hum seems thin, like a thread pulled too tight.

beats.scene: A tall stranger in the dawn lane holds a lantern without a flame
beats.summary: At dawn a tall stranger named Master Pike arrives in the lane with a lantern that burns without oil.

beats.scene: The stranger kneels beside a lamp post and listens with his head tilted
beats.summary: The stranger listens to the village lamp as Wren does, and says it has been humming to someone for a long time.

beats.scene: Alder opens the cottage door while the stranger bows politely
beats.summary: Alder greets Master Ostrander Pike with caution, and invites him in for porridge; Wren stares from the stairs.

beats.scene: Pike sits at a cottage table with a bowl of porridge, steam rising
beats.summary: Over porridge, Pike explains that he teaches Listening at a school far away, and has come looking for a particular kind of child.

beats.scene: Pike places a small grey stone in Wren's open hand
beats.summary: Pike takes a small grey stone from his pocket and places it in Wren's palm.

beats.scene: Wren closes her fingers around the stone, her eyes wide with surprise
beats.summary: The stone hums in Wren's hand, and when she hums back, it answers her; she has never been answered before.

beats.scene: Pike speaks to Wren and Alder, a painted map of mountains on the table
beats.summary: Pike describes the Academy Under the Mountain in Orrenfell, where children who hear the Hum are taught to listen.

beats.scene: Alder crosses his arms and frowns at Pike across the table
beats.summary: Alder asks hard questions about the distance, the danger and the cost; Pike answers each one honestly.

beats.scene: Alder stands alone by the last lamp in the lane at twilight
beats.summary: Alder walks out alone to the last lamp in the lane to think, while Wren watches from the window.

beats.scene: Father and daughter sit by the fire, his hand on her shoulder
beats.summary: That night Alder tells Wren that a gift needs a place to grow, and that he can light the lamps alone.

beats.scene: Wren packs a small bag while her father hands her a brass key
beats.summary: Wren packs her small bag, and her father gives her a small brass lamp-key from his first ladder.

beats.scene: Neighbours gather at the gate in the early light, a mule waiting
beats.summary: Neighbours gather to see her off; Dill Hobbs says nothing, and old Mags Fenner gives Wren a woollen scarf.

beats.scene: Wren hugs her father at the village gate as a mule waits behind them
beats.summary: Wren hugs her father at the gate, and leaves on a mule with Master Pike as the lamps behind them hum goodbye.

beats.scene: Two mules walk along a winding road between dark pine trees
beats.summary: Wren rides Dumpling the mule behind Pike's mule Sorrel, through the pine woods at the foot of Orrenfell.

beats.scene: Wren and Pike eat bread beside a stream tumbling over mossy stones
beats.summary: At a stream, Wren hears the water hum, and Pike teaches her the first rule of Listening: listen first.

beats.scene: Pike's lantern glows among the pine trunks as stars appear overhead
beats.summary: At night in camp, Pike's lantern glows without oil, and he tells Wren the Hum lives in all things and can be held and lent.

beats.scene: Wren stands on a stony slope with her boot pressed to the ground
beats.summary: On the second morning Pike teaches Wren to feel the mountain's deep hum through her boots.

beats.scene: A hawk circles above bare grey slopes as the mules climb
beats.summary: On bare slopes above the trees, Wren hears the hum of a hawk overhead and the faint hum of the grass.

beats.scene: A low stone hut stands among rocks, goats gathered at its door
beats.summary: They reach Crow's Rest, a stone hut where old Nan Crowe keeps goats and gives travellers shelter.

beats.scene: Nan Crowe talks quietly to Pike by the stove while Wren pretends to sleep
beats.summary: In the night Wren overhears Nan tell Pike that the mountain's songs have been growing thin; Pike asks her to be quiet.

beats.scene: Mules climb into drifting cloud on a narrow path beside high cliffs
beats.summary: On the third day the party climbs into cloud, so low that it hangs below their heads.

beats.scene: Wren sits on a rock, anxious, as Pike kneels in front of her
beats.summary: Wren fears the Academy will not want her; Pike says the Great Door opens only to a hum, and hers is a true one.

beats.scene: A vast stone door carved with lamps stands closed in the cliff face
beats.summary: The clouds part to reveal a huge stone door set into the cliff, carved with lamps; it is closed and silent.

beats.scene: Wren faces the huge stone door while Pike steps back behind her
beats.summary: Pike tells Wren that the Great Door cannot be pushed or pulled; it must be asked, and he steps back to let her try.

beats.scene: Wren hums to the silent door, her eyes shut tight
beats.summary: Wren hums at the door as loudly as she can, but nothing happens, until she remembers the first rule: listen first.

beats.scene: Wren stands with her palm on the stone as carved lamps begin to glow
beats.summary: Wren listens, hears the door's own deep hum, and matches it softly; the carved lamps start to glow one by one.

beats.scene: The Great Door swings slowly open and warm golden light pours out
beats.summary: The Great Door swings open for Wren, and a warm golden light spills out over the stony ground.

beats.scene: An old man with a broom leads two mules into a lamplit stable cave
beats.summary: Inside the door, the old caretaker Ibb takes the mules, and says the door has not opened so quickly in years.

beats.scene: A vast cavern city glitters with thousands of lamps, bridges and glowing moss
beats.summary: Down a tunnel of glowing moss, Wren sees the Academy: a cavern city of lamps, stone bridges and moss, deep in the mountain.

beats.scene: Wren and Pike cross a long stone bridge above a deep dark space
beats.summary: Crossing a bridge, Pike tells Wren that the Heartstone, a crystal at the mountain's heart, gives the Academy its light.

beats.scene: Thirty nervous children stand together in a great hall lit by lamps
beats.summary: In the Hall of Lamps, about thirty new students from all over the land wait nervously for the Warden.

beats.scene: A tall woman in a grey gown walks into a hushed hall
beats.summary: Warden Isolde Marrow, head of the Academy, enters the hall; her voice is calm and serious and rings like a bell.

beats.scene: The Warden raises three fingers before the hushed new students
beats.summary: Warden Marrow gives the three rules: listen first, never go below the Ninth Stair, give back what you borrow.

beats.scene: New students follow a lamp-bearing guide up a winding stair
beats.summary: After the Warden's welcome, an older student leads the new children up winding stairs to the Sixth Gallery.

beats.scene: Wren pushes open a round door into a bedroom with three beds
beats.summary: Wren finds her room, round and warm, with three beds, three chests and a window of glowing moss.

beats.scene: A girl with folded arms sits on the bed beside the window
beats.summary: Priya Anand, already in the room, claims the bed by the window and warns Wren not to touch her blanket.

beats.scene: Priya hums while a patch of frost melts across the stone floor
beats.summary: Priya says she comes from the far city of Velmara, and without thinking melts a patch of frost on the floor with her hum.

beats.scene: A boy with a heavy trunk and a loaf stands in the doorway
beats.summary: Tobias Kettle, a baker's son from Lowmarket, arrives nervous and out of breath, with a loaf of bread under his arm.

beats.scene: Three children share a loaf of bread sitting on the patchwork rug
beats.summary: The three roommates share Tobe's bread, and Wren says she is a lamplighter's daughter; Priya says that is wonderful.

beats.scene: Three beds in a dim round room as the moss glows softly at night
beats.summary: On the first night the moss dims to a gentle glow; Wren feels homesick, and Tobe counts out loud to help them sleep.

beats.scene: A tall boy sneers across a long breakfast table
beats.summary: At the first breakfast, a proud boy named Cassian Vale sneers at Wren's muddy village boots.

beats.scene: Priya glares and frost spreads across Cassian's bowl
beats.summary: Priya answers Cassian sharply, and frost creeps over his bowl until Tobe tugs her sleeve.

beats.scene: A timetable is pinned to the wall beside the dining hall door
beats.summary: A timetable on the wall shows the first lessons; Wren reads that Listening with Master Pike comes first.

beats.scene: Students sit on cushions in a round grey room with a high ceiling
beats.summary: The first lesson is held in the Quiet Room, a round grey chamber where Pike waits with his oil-less lantern.

beats.scene: Pike places a small pebble into each student's hands
beats.summary: Pike hands every student a plain pebble and sets the first task: sit in silence and find the pebble's hum.

beats.scene: Students fidget and sigh in the long silence as Tobe's stomach rumbles
beats.summary: The silence stretches; students fidget, Priya scratches her nose, and Tobe's stomach rumbles loudly.

beats.scene: Wren closes her eyes, her small pebble resting in her open palm
beats.summary: Wren closes her eyes and finds her pebble's hum quickly: a gentle, round note like a bee asleep.

beats.scene: Cassian scowls at his pebble as it rattles against his knee
beats.summary: Cassian's hum is strong but harsh, and his pebble buzzes and rattles off his knee onto the floor.

beats.scene: Pike speaks to Cassian beside the rolling pebble while Wren watches
beats.summary: Pike tells Cassian that a strong hum is a fine thing, but a hammer is for building and not for listening; Cassian blames Wren.

beats.scene: Tobe stands at the cave mouth with his hands over his ears
beats.summary: Tobe is afraid to send his hum into the dark, and freezes at the mouth of the cave with his hands over his ears.

beats.scene: Wren holds Tobe's hand at the cave as a counting echo returns
beats.summary: Wren holds Tobe's hand and suggests he hum his counting; the cave sings the numbers back, and he laughs.

beats.scene: Priya holds out her hands as frost melts across a stone floor
beats.summary: In Tuning class Priya's quick hum calms a sheet of frost, and Pike shows the friends how stones can be tuned like strings.

beats.scene: Three friends kneel round stones on a patchwork rug, laughing
beats.summary: That evening the three friends practise tuning pebbles on the rug, and Wren writes her first letter home.

beats.scene: A quiet grey-haired man stands beside a wall of rough stone in a classroom
beats.summary: Master Corvin Hale, the teacher of Stone, is quiet and sad; Cassian, his nephew, sits very straight in the front row.

beats.scene: Hale lays his palm flat on the stone wall as the class watches
beats.summary: Hale tells the class that stones remember every song sung to them, and his voice breaks as he says it.

beats.scene: Wren walks between tall shelves where glowing books whisper
beats.summary: Wren discovers the Hall of Held Breath, the Academy's library, where tall shelves rise into the dark and the books whisper.

beats.scene: Wren sits still in a reading chair as a thin blue book glows
beats.summary: The books whisper only to a patient reader; when Wren sits quietly, a thin blue book tells her how the first lamp was lit.

beats.scene: Wren reads at a long table beneath a hanging lamp, a thick book open
beats.summary: Wren spends her free hours in the Hall and learns of the Heartstone, a crystal whose hum has lit the Academy for a thousand years.

beats.scene: Priya and Tobe find Wren among the shelves, Tobe holding a whispering book
beats.summary: Priya and Tobe find Wren in the library; Tobe's book whispers number puzzles, and Priya complains that she cannot sit still.

beats.scene: Ibb sweeps the floor beside the children as a lamp glows nearby
beats.summary: Ibb the caretaker, who knows all the legends, tells the friends that some questions are better kept until the right time.

beats.scene: A long-legged courier hands Wren a letter at the Great Door
beats.summary: A letter arrives from Alder: the lamps of Hollin Ford are all lit, and Dill Hobbs has asked after her.

beats.scene: Cassian reads alone at a far table in the library, hunched over a book
beats.summary: One evening Wren sees Cassian reading alone in the library, and he leaves quickly when he notices her looking.

beats.scene: The whispering books fall silent all at once in the dim library
beats.summary: That night, all the whispering books in the Hall go quiet at once, and Wren feels a strange chill.

beats.scene: Wren walks alone along the lamplit Sixth Gallery, then slows and stops
beats.summary: Wren hurries back to the Sixth Gallery, and one stretch of floor beneath the lamps feels strangely cold.

beats.scene: Wren kneels in a lamplit gallery with her ear against the stone floor
beats.summary: Wren puts her ear to the floor and hears a wrong silence, as though a part of the hum had been cut away.

beats.scene: Wren sits in Tuning class with a frown while the other students hum
beats.summary: Now that Wren has heard the wrong silence, she hears it everywhere, and she cannot concentrate in Tuning class.

beats.scene: Wren stands in a small office crowded with softly humming lanterns
beats.summary: After class Pike asks Wren to stay, and takes her to his small office full of lanterns.

beats.scene: Master Pike sits opposite Wren, his grave face lit by lanterns
beats.summary: Pike admits that the Heartstone has been growing quiet for months, and asks Wren to say nothing for now.

beats.scene: Pike hands Wren a small leather notebook across his desk
beats.summary: Pike teaches Wren to map the silences, writing down where and when each one appears.

beats.scene: Wren sits on her bed while Priya studies her face with narrowed eyes
beats.summary: Wren keeps the secret from Priya and Tobe; Priya notices she is distracted, and Wren says she is only homesick.

beats.scene: Master Hale stands before a flickering lamp as students watch
beats.summary: In Stone class a lamp flickers, and Hale, thin and tired with dark shadows under his eyes, leaves abruptly.

beats.scene: Cassian stands before Wren in a corridor with his arms crossed
beats.summary: Cassian challenges Wren to a hum contest, calling her village-made; Wren politely refuses.

beats.scene: Snow drifts down through a high shaft of rock far above the cavern
beats.summary: The first snow of winter drifts down through the high Skylight Shaft, and the whole school talks about Lantern Night.

beats.scene: Students polish small brass lamps in a busy workshop cave
beats.summary: In the weeks before Lantern Night, every student polishes a small lamp, which they must light from their own hum.

beats.scene: Three friends practise on the patchwork rug with three unlit lamps
beats.summary: The friends practise at night but can only make small sparks; Priya's sparks are silver, Tobe's are gold, and Wren's are blue.

beats.scene: Snow falls into the dark Hall of Lamps as the Warden holds a candle
beats.summary: On Lantern Night, snow falls into the dark Hall of Lamps, and Warden Marrow says each student will light a lamp with their own hum.

beats.scene: Priya lights a lamp that burns with a pale silver flame
beats.summary: Priya lights her lamp with a pale silver flame that sparkles like frost, and the hall applauds.

beats.scene: Tobe lights a lamp that burns with a steady golden flame
beats.summary: Tobe counts under his breath and lights a steady, warm golden flame, and he almost cannot believe it.

beats.scene: Wren's small brass lamp burns with a bright blue flame
beats.summary: Wren listens first, then hums; her lamp burns bright blue, and the whole hall falls silent.

beats.scene: Warden Marrow and Master Pike exchange a look beside a blue lamp
beats.summary: The Warden stares at the blue flame with wide eyes, and Pike looks both glad and troubled.

beats.scene: Cassian's lamp sputters and gutters out as he clenches his fists
beats.summary: Cassian's lamp gutters and goes out twice, because he hums too hard, and the hall grows uncomfortable.

beats.scene: Cassian points at Wren in the dark hall as students whisper
beats.summary: Cassian blames Wren, saying she hummed over him; Warden Marrow calmly says nobody can take another's hum by listening.

beats.scene: Two students sweep a soot-black tunnel lined with dead lamps
beats.summary: As a punishment for the quarrel, Wren and Cassian must clean the lamp tunnels together every evening for a week.

beats.scene: Two students carry buckets into a low tunnel lined with sooty lamps
beats.summary: On the first evening, Wren and Cassian carry buckets and cloths into the lamp tunnels, and scrub in an icy silence.

beats.scene: Cassian drops a dirty cloth into a bucket and glares at Wren
beats.summary: Cassian says Wren thinks she is special, and Wren says she only listens; they quarrel in whispers.

beats.scene: Ibb sets down a pot of tea in the tunnel mouth and chuckles
beats.summary: Ibb brings them hot tea and says that lamp soot is the breath of the mountain, and that tunnels have long memories.

beats.scene: Wren shows Cassian how to listen to a lamp while he cleans it
beats.summary: On the third evening Wren shows Cassian how to listen to a lamp before touching it, and the soot lifts easily.

beats.scene: Wren and Cassian stand before a row of lit but silent lamps
beats.summary: On the fifth evening, Wren and Cassian find a stretch of lamps that are lit but have no hum at all.

beats.scene: Cassian leans close to a silent lamp with a startled expression
beats.summary: To her astonishment Cassian says in a low voice that he can feel the silence too.

beats.scene: Wren and Cassian crouch in the tunnel, speaking in whispers
beats.summary: They agree to keep quiet until they know more; Cassian says his uncle has hardly slept since the autumn.

beats.scene: Students wake in the dark as the lamps of a gallery fail
beats.summary: In the night, the lamps of the Fifth Gallery fail, and the glowing moss fades; students wake in the cold dark.

beats.scene: Students huddle with candles as Warden Marrow sings in the dark
beats.summary: Warden Marrow arrives with a candle and sings a calm song that settles the frightened students.

beats.scene: Four children sit together in a dark corridor after the lights return
beats.summary: Wren tells Priya and Tobe about the silences and apologises for the lie; Priya forgives her, and Cassian asks to join them.

beats.scene: Four children kneel around a large map spread on the library floor
beats.summary: The four friends spread a map of the galleries on the library floor, and Tobe marks every silence from Wren's notebook with chalk.

beats.scene: Tobe points his chalk along a line of crosses leading downward on the map
beats.summary: The crosses make a pattern: they begin near the top of the Academy and lead, gallery by gallery, toward the Ninth Stair.

beats.scene: Priya draws a line of frost across a gallery floor as Wren watches
beats.summary: Priya tests the silences by drawing a line of frost across the floor, and finds that frost will not form where the hum is cut.

beats.scene: Cassian presses a hand on the floor with his jaw set in concentration
beats.summary: Cassian's strong hum proves useful: he can feel the edges of a silence as a blunt pressure, and the friends begin to accept him.

beats.scene: Four children crouch in a dark gallery, wrapped in blankets, one holding bread
beats.summary: The friends take turns to keep watch at night in the Fifth Gallery, wrapped in blankets, with Tobe supplying bread.

beats.scene: A cloaked figure carries a glass jar along a dim gallery
beats.summary: On the fourth night, a cloaked figure appears carrying a glass jar and holds it against a lamp.

beats.scene: A thread of silver light flows from a lamp into a glass jar
beats.summary: The hum of the lamp is drawn into the jar as a thread of light, and the lamp goes silent.

beats.scene: The cloaked figure turns toward the hidden children in a dark gallery
beats.summary: Priya gasps, the figure turns to the sound, and bolts away in the dark with the jar.

beats.scene: Children race through winding galleries with a cloaked figure ahead
beats.summary: The friends chase the figure through winding galleries, with Tobe counting turns and Cassian shouting to halt.

beats.scene: A cloaked figure vanishes into a blank stone wall
beats.summary: The figure runs into a blank stone wall and vanishes into it, leaving a folded page fluttering on the floor.

beats.scene: Wren unfolds a page showing a drawing of a great crystal
beats.summary: Wren unfolds the page: it shows a drawing of a great crystal at the end of a spiral stair, with a few lines of writing beneath.

beats.scene: Wren holds the page toward a lantern as Cassian leans in over her shoulder
beats.summary: The words under the drawing say that when the mountain is quiet, she will wake; Cassian turns pale at the handwriting.

beats.scene: Cassian walks quickly away down a dark gallery, leaving the friends behind
beats.summary: Cassian takes the page, studies the writing, and walks away without a word; Wren lies awake that night, wondering.

beats.scene: Cassian sits alone on a stone step with a small lamp beside him
beats.summary: The next evening Wren finds Cassian sitting alone on a quiet stair, and sits down quietly beside him.

beats.scene: Cassian touches the folded page with one finger, his face turned away
beats.summary: Cassian says the handwriting is his uncle's, Master Hale's, which he knows from monthly letters.

beats.scene: Cassian looks into the distance on the stone step, a lamp glowing
beats.summary: Cassian explains that his parents are mapmakers who are always away, and that his uncle was once warm and kind to him.

beats.scene: Wren and Cassian walk back through a gallery toward the Sixth Gallery
beats.summary: Wren tells Cassian that they must learn the truth before blaming anyone, and Cassian asks her not to tell anyone yet.

beats.scene: Priya and Tobe look at Cassian as he explains by the mossy window
beats.summary: Cassian tells Priya and Tobe about the handwriting, and Tobe suggests asking Ibb, who knows every old story in the mountain.

beats.scene: Ibb sits by a small fire in the stable cave, four children around him
beats.summary: In the warm stable cave, Ibb pokes the fire and tells the four of them the story of Elin Hale.

beats.scene: Ibb talks by the fire, his face half in shadow
beats.summary: Ibb tells how thirty years ago Elin Hale, Master Hale's daughter and the best listener of her year, went below the Ninth Stair and was never seen again.

beats.scene: Four children walk slowly along a dim gallery, talking in low voices
beats.summary: Walking back from Ibb's cave, the friends wonder whether the she in the page means Elin, and Cassian says his uncle must hope to wake her.

beats.scene: Snow gathers on the ledges as students huddle over soup in the dining hall
beats.summary: Winter deepens; the cuts continue elsewhere, the figure does not return to the Fifth Gallery, and the friends keep marking their map.

beats.scene: Master Pike stands before the class in the Quiet Room, raising one finger
beats.summary: Pike announces the Long Note, the spring test of patience: holding a single hum for a whole hour.

beats.scene: Students sit in rows with their eyes shut and their cheeks puffed
beats.summary: The first attempts are short: students manage a few minutes, Priya sneezes at three, and Tobe counts to keep going.

beats.scene: Cassian hums with a red face while his note shakes and cracks
beats.summary: Cassian's harsh hum cracks at four minutes; Pike tells him that the Long Note is not about strength but about softness.

beats.scene: Wren sits cross-legged in a corner, eyes closed, a faint smile on her face
beats.summary: Wren discovers a trick: she hums slowly like her father's lamp breathing, and holds the note for twenty minutes.

beats.scene: Cassian hums softly in an empty tunnel while Wren listens beside him
beats.summary: Wren helps Cassian practise a softer hum in the lamp tunnels, and he holds a note for ten minutes with tears of joy.

beats.scene: Tobe stands in the Echo cave counting out loud while numbers ring back
beats.summary: In Echo class, Tobe's counting turns into a beautiful long song, and he holds a note for half an hour without noticing.

beats.scene: Water drips from the ceiling of a tunnel as the snow begins to melt
beats.summary: The first thaw comes; the mountain's hum becomes a trickling song, and a letter from Alder arrives with a pressed snowdrop.

beats.scene: Four friends sit in a circle on the patchwork rug, their hands joined
beats.summary: The friends promise each other on the rug that they will hold the Long Note for an hour, and learn the truth of the silences.

beats.scene: First-year students line up with lanterns beside Master Hale and Mistress Brook
beats.summary: A spring trip is announced to the Singing Falls, led by Master Hale and Mistress Brook, and the first years set out with lanterns.

beats.scene: Students walk down a damp tunnel as a distant roar grows louder
beats.summary: The group walks through a long damp tunnel, and a distant roaring grows louder until it seems to shake the walls.

beats.scene: A huge underground waterfall plunges into a dark lake, glowing with spray
beats.summary: They come out above the Singing Falls, a huge underground waterfall that plunges into a dark lake and sings in many voices.

beats.scene: Students send their humming toward the falling water in a row
beats.summary: Mistress Brook teaches that water remembers songs, and each student sends a note to join the falls.

beats.scene: Master Hale stands apart at the edge of the ledge, staring into the water
beats.summary: Master Hale stands apart, staring into the falls with a lost look, and Cassian watches him closely.

beats.scene: Wren listens with her head tilted toward the falls, frowning
beats.summary: Wren listens to the Falls and hears a thin gap in their song, the same kind of silence as in the lamps.

beats.scene: Wren whispers to her three friends on the ledge while spray drifts around them
beats.summary: Wren whispers the news to her friends, and Tobe frowns, trying to remember something about the nights.

beats.scene: Tobe counts on his fingers with chalk in hand, his notebook open
beats.summary: Tobe counts the nights from Wren's notebook and finds that the cuts come every ninth night.

beats.scene: Tobe points at a date in the notebook while the friends lean close
beats.summary: The next ninth night will fall on a Thursday, and the friends realise that they might catch the thief.

beats.scene: Pike hands a small brass bell to Wren across his desk of lanterns
beats.summary: They tell Pike about the pattern; he says the Warden is away until Friday, and gives them a bell to ring if they see anyone near the Ninth Stair.

beats.scene: Four children make careful plans over a small lantern on the patchwork rug
beats.summary: On Wednesday night the friends make a plan, and Cassian asks what happens if he is wrong about his uncle.

beats.scene: Master Hale stands in a classroom with a stone slab, looking tired and gentle
beats.summary: On Thursday Hale teaches Stone class gently and calmly, and before the class ends he tells Cassian to take care of himself.

beats.scene: A high stone balcony looks over a dark stairway at night
beats.summary: In the evening the four friends hide behind the stone balustrade of the Eighth Gallery, which overlooks the stair to the lower levels.

beats.scene: Four children share bread as frost creeps over the stone rail
beats.summary: They wait in the cold; Priya's frost creeps over the rail, Tobe counts the hours, and Wren hears a thread of hum.

beats.scene: A great bell tolls midnight in the vast dark cavern
beats.summary: A deep bell tolls midnight across the cavern, and the four friends go very still.

beats.scene: A cloaked man climbs a dark stair with a basket of jars
beats.summary: A figure in a cloak appears at the foot of the great stair, carrying a basket that clinks with empty glass jars.

beats.scene: The hood slips back to show Master Hale's tired face in the lamplight
beats.summary: As the figure passes under a lamp, the hood slips, and it is Master Hale; Cassian whispers uncle, and Wren takes his arm.

beats.scene: Hale holds a jar to a lamp as silver light flows in
beats.summary: Hale draws a lamp's hum into a jar with trembling hands, and murmurs that soon he will see his daughter.

beats.scene: Cassian takes the brass bell with a shaking hand
beats.summary: After a long struggle Cassian takes the bell from Wren, and rings it with all his courage, so that its clear note carries through the galleries.

beats.scene: Master Hale looks up in alarm on a stone stair, dropping his basket
beats.summary: Hale hears the bell and looks up in alarm; then he gathers the jars and hurries down the Ninth Stair.

beats.scene: A rusty chain hangs across the top of a dark stair
beats.summary: At the top of the Ninth Stair, a rusty chain hangs across the opening, and the friends remember the second rule.

beats.scene: Wren stands at the chain, listening with her eyes shut
beats.summary: Wren listens to what the mountain says, and decides that the first rule of listening matters more than a chain.

beats.scene: Four children climb over a rusty chain and begin to descend
beats.summary: They climb over the chain one by one, and Tobe, trembling, begins to count the steps aloud.

beats.scene: A narrow spiral stair winds downward with blue-green moss on the walls
beats.summary: The spiral stair winds down and down; the moss turns from green to deep blue, and the hum deepens like a slow heartbeat.

beats.scene: Priya scatters frost on slippery wet steps as the others follow
beats.summary: Lower down the steps are wet and slippery, and Priya scatters a fine frost on them so that the group can walk safely.

beats.scene: Wren reads words scratched into the stone wall by lantern light
beats.summary: On the wall Wren finds words scratched long ago: Elin Hale was here, aged fifteen; Cassian stares at it in silence.

beats.scene: Tobe stands on a step counting aloud, a faint echo returning from below
beats.summary: Tobe's counting echoes from below, telling them how close the bottom is, and Wren hears Hale's footsteps stop.

beats.scene: Four children stand before a huge arched black door
beats.summary: At the bottom, they find a great arched door of black stone traced with silver lines, with Master Hale standing before it.

beats.scene: Master Hale turns, his face sad and tired, before the door
beats.summary: Hale turns to the children, not angry, and tells them why: his daughter's echo is hidden under the Heartstone's loud song, and he hoped silence would let her wake.

beats.scene: Hale presses his palm against the carved black door as light seeps out
beats.summary: Hale lays his palm on the door, which swings open slowly, and a pale glow spills out of the Hollow.

beats.scene: A vast domed chamber holds a huge crystal glowing faintly and unsteadily
beats.summary: The door opens on the Hollow, a vast domed chamber where the Heartstone, a crystal as big as a house, glows faintly and unsteadily.

beats.scene: Hale sets down his basket of jars near the foot of the huge crystal
beats.summary: Hale sets his basket down near the crystal, and the jars whisper and flicker as if they know where they are.

beats.scene: Wren puts her ear against the cool surface of a huge crystal
beats.summary: Wren crosses the floor and lays her ear against the Heartstone, where a pale light moves slowly inside.

beats.scene: Wren listens with closed eyes as a pale light circles inside the stone
beats.summary: Wren understands that the hum travels in a circle from the Heartstone to every lamp and back, and that the jars have broken the circle.

beats.scene: Wren turns from the crystal toward Hale, her hands open
beats.summary: Wren tells Hale gently what she has heard; Hale says he only wanted to borrow a little, and was never going to keep it.

beats.scene: A girl's faint shape shimmers inside the crystal as Wren listens
beats.summary: Wren listens deeper and hears, far below the great hum, a girl's voice, which is Elin's echo, saying that the song must go home.

beats.scene: Wren speaks quietly to Hale while he stands motionless in the glow
beats.summary: Wren tells Hale what Elin's echo said, in the exact words, and Hale stands very still.

beats.scene: Hale kneels before the glowing crystal as Cassian rests a hand on his shoulder
beats.summary: Hale kneels and weeps, and Cassian takes his hand and says, in a steady voice, that it is time to give back what he has borrowed.

beats.scene: Glass jars open one by one on the floor, releasing threads of silver light
beats.summary: Hale opens the jars one by one, and the stolen hum rises in threads of silver light and flows toward the Heartstone.

beats.scene: Four children and an old teacher stand around a crystal, singing together
beats.summary: Wren, Priya, Tobe and Cassian lend their own hums, and together with Hale they sing to the Heartstone.

beats.scene: Pike and Warden Marrow lead a crowd down into the chamber
beats.summary: The bell has woken the whole Academy, and Pike and the Warden, who has returned early, hurry down the Ninth Stair with many students.

beats.scene: The Warden raises her hand in the doorway of the great chamber
beats.summary: At the door of the Hollow they stop, astonished, and the Warden raises a hand for silence.

beats.scene: Teachers and students stand in a wide circle singing in a vast chamber
beats.summary: One by one, Pike, Mistress Brook, Ibb and the students join the song, and the Hollow fills with voices.

beats.scene: The Heartstone blazes golden-white as students shield their eyes
beats.summary: The song grows until it seems to shake the stone, and the Heartstone begins to blaze with golden-white light.

beats.scene: A girl's figure made of light rises from inside a glowing crystal
beats.summary: A girl's shape of light rises from the heart of the Heartstone: Elin's echo, fifteen years old, just as she was.

beats.scene: The glowing girl looks at Master Hale with kind eyes
beats.summary: Elin's echo speaks to her father in a clear, warm voice: she was never lost, only listening, and she thanks him for waiting.

beats.scene: Hale reaches toward the glowing girl as a golden light surrounds them both
beats.summary: Hale says her name; Elin smiles at Cassian, and asks her father to give the song to others, as he gave it to her.

beats.scene: The glowing girl fades into golden mist inside the crystal
beats.summary: Elin's echo thanks everyone and fades peacefully into the Heartstone's light, like the last note of a song.

beats.scene: Wren stands with her hand on the glowing crystal, eyes shining
beats.summary: The circle closes: the hum of the Heartstone is whole again, deep and steady, and Wren feels the mountain's gratitude.

beats.scene: Lamps flare up along bridges and stairs across a vast cavern at dawn
beats.summary: Across the Academy the lamps blaze up again, the moss glows green, and the cold lifts from every gallery.

beats.scene: Students climb a spiral stair toward dawn; an old man waits
beats.summary: The whole company climbs the Ninth Stair together, and at the top Ibb is waiting with a pot of tea and a smile.

beats.scene: Master Hale stands before Warden Marrow in her lamplit study, his head bowed
beats.summary: In the Warden's study Hale tells her the whole truth, and the four children stand beside him to say what they did.

beats.scene: Warden Marrow sits at her desk speaking gently to a grey-haired man
beats.summary: The Warden does not send Hale away; she gives him the care of the Heartstone, and tells the children their courage was greater than their obedience, but not a reason to ignore rules.

beats.scene: The Warden stands before the school in the great hall, speaking calmly
beats.summary: The Warden announces a new tradition: every spring the whole school will sing to the mountain, so the Academy always gives back.

beats.scene: The whole school sings together beneath thousands of glowing lamps
beats.summary: Everyone gathers to sing for the first Giving Back, and the thousand lamps hum along as one great choir.

beats.scene: Cassian and Wren share bread side by side on a high bridge
beats.summary: Cassian finds Wren on a high bridge, apologises for laughing at her boots and for the unkind things that followed, and they become friends.

beats.scene: Master Hale and Cassian play chess in a lamplit gallery
beats.summary: Master Hale begins to smile again, plays chess with Cassian in the evenings, and teaches Stone with a new warmth.

beats.scene: Four friends laugh together in a mossy gallery, each holding a lamp
beats.summary: Tobe, Priya, Cassian and Wren spend the weeks before the test together; Tobe maps every lamp, and Priya freezes a pond for them to slide on.

beats.scene: Students sit in rows in the Quiet Room with their eyes closed
beats.summary: On the day of the Long Note test, the first years sit in the Quiet Room, and Pike tells them that the test is about giving, not winning.

beats.scene: Wren sits cross-legged in a quiet hall as an hourglass runs low
beats.summary: Wren holds the Long Note for a whole hour by thinking of her father's lamp, and passes the test.

beats.scene: Students sit at long tables beneath thousands of lanterns at a feast
beats.summary: Priya, Tobe and Cassian also pass the Long Note, and the school holds a farewell feast under thousands of lamps.

beats.scene: Priya and Tobe stand on a stone bridge, holding a ribbon and a loaf
beats.summary: Priya gives Wren a blue ribbon, Tobe gives her a loaf, and they promise to meet again in the autumn.

beats.scene: Wren pats a mule in the stable cave while Ibb leans on his broom
beats.summary: Wren says goodbye to Ibb in the stable cave, and he tells her that giving back is the whole of it.

beats.scene: Cassian hands Wren a small folded map in a quiet gallery
beats.summary: Cassian gives Wren a map of the Academy that he drew himself, and says that he will see her in autumn.

beats.scene: Master Pike hands Wren a small lantern at the Great Door
beats.summary: Before she goes home for the summer, Pike gives Wren a small lantern of her own, which hums to her alone.

beats.scene: The Great Door swings open as Wren hums at it and sunlight pours in
beats.summary: The Great Door opens at once to Wren's hum, and she rides Dumpling out into the spring sunlight.

beats.scene: A girl on a mule rides down a long green mountain path
beats.summary: Wren rides down the mountain with Pike for three days, and hears the mountain's hum growing fainter behind her, and the lamps of the valley rising ahead.

beats.scene: Dill Hobbs stands at the village gate at dusk, cap in hand
beats.summary: In Hollin Ford, Dill Hobbs awkwardly says hello and asks what the mountain is like; Wren tells him, and he does not laugh.

beats.scene: Wren runs down a lane toward her father, who waits beside a ladder
beats.summary: Wren runs down the lane and throws her arms around her father, and shows him her lantern; he says the lamps have missed her.

beats.scene: Wren lights the first lamp of evening in her village as stars appear
beats.summary: In Hollin Ford, Wren and her father light the first lamp of evening, and she hears the mountain's hum inside it; she will return in autumn.

A1A2: Every evening, Wren listened to the soft song inside the lamps.
Wren followed her father as he lit the lamps along the lane.
The old stone wall by the well hummed too, but more slowly.
The village children laughed and called her Wall-Ear.
That night, Wren asked her father if she was strange.
One night, all the lamps hummed towards the dark mountain in the north.
Wren could not sleep, so she put her ear to the window.
At dawn, a tall stranger stood in the lane with a lantern.
The stranger put his ear to a lamp, just like Wren.
Her father opened the door, and the stranger bowed politely.
Master Pike sat at the table and ate a big bowl of bread and milk.
Pike took a small grey stone out of his pocket.
The stone was humming, and it hummed back when she did.
Pike told them about a school inside the great mountain.
Her father asked many questions about the journey and the school.
Her father went out alone to stand by the last lamp.
That night, her father said she should go to the school.
Wren packed a small bag, and her father gave her a key.
Neighbours came to the gate, and one old woman gave her a scarf.
Wren hugged her father tightly and rode away on a mule.
Wren rode a mule called Dumpling into the dark pine woods.
By a stream, Pike told her to listen before she spoke.
That night, Pike's lantern glowed without any oil or flame.
On the second morning, Pike taught her to hear the mountain.
A hawk flew high above them, and Wren heard its hum.
At sunset, they reached a small stone hut full of goats.
At night, Wren heard Nan say the mountain was growing quiet.
On the third day, they rode up into the cold clouds.
Wren was afraid the school would not want her.
Then the clouds opened, and she saw a huge stone door.
Pike said that the door must be asked, not pushed.
Wren hummed loudly at the door, but nothing happened at all.
She listened, and heard the deep hum of the door itself.
The great door swung open, and warm golden light poured out.
An old man with a broom took their mules away.
At the end of the tunnel lay a huge cave full of lamps.
Pike said a great crystal far below gave the city its light.
In a great hall, thirty new students waited with her.
Then the Warden walked in, and the whole hall went silent.
She gave them three rules to keep while they lived there.
An older student led them up a long, winding stair.
Her room was round, with three beds and a glowing window.
A girl sat on the bed by the window with folded arms.
Priya came from a far city, and she could melt frost.
A nervous boy arrived with a heavy trunk and a loaf.
The three children sat on the rug and shared Tobe's bread.
That night, Wren missed her father, and Tobe began to count.
At breakfast, a proud boy laughed at Wren's village boots.
Priya looked hard at him, and frost spread over his bowl.
The timetable said they would have Listening class first.
The Quiet Room was round and grey, and very, very still.
Master Pike gave each student a plain grey pebble to hold.
The silence grew long, and Tobe's stomach made a loud noise.
Wren shut her eyes and soon heard her pebble's quiet hum.
Cassian's pebble shook and jumped off his knee.
Pike told Cassian that listening is not the same as hitting.
In Echo class, Tobe was afraid of the dark cave.
Wren held his hand, and the cave sang his numbers back.
Priya hummed, and a sheet of frost melted away.
That evening, the friends practised with stones, and Wren wrote home.
Master Hale taught Stone class, and he looked very sad.
Hale said that stones remember every song they have heard.
Wren found a huge library where the books whispered.
Wren sat still, and a blue book began to whisper to her.
Wren read about the great crystal at the heart of the mountain.
Priya and Tobe found Wren, and Tobe's book whispered numbers.
Old Ibb swept the floor and listened to their questions.
A letter came from her father, and Wren read it twice.
Wren saw Cassian reading alone, and he quickly went away.
That night, all the books in the library stopped whispering.
Wren walked back along the gallery, then stopped in surprise.
She put her ear to the floor and heard a strange silence.
Now Wren heard strange gaps in the hum everywhere she went.
After class, Pike took Wren to his small office.
Pike told her the great crystal was growing quiet.
Pike showed Wren how to write down where the silences were.
Priya asked what was wrong, but Wren did not say.
In Stone class, a lamp went dim, and Hale left suddenly.
Cassian wanted a hum contest, but Wren said no.
Snow fell through a hole high above the great cave.
Before Lantern Night, each student polished a small brass lamp.
The three friends practised at night, but their lamps stayed dark.
On Lantern Night, the Warden stood in a dark, snowy hall.
Priya went first, and her lamp burned with a silver flame.
Tobe counted softly, and his lamp burned with a golden flame.
Wren's lamp burned with a bright blue flame, and the hall went still.
The Warden stared at the blue flame, and Pike looked worried.
Cassian's lamp shook and then went out completely.
Cassian said Wren had stolen his hum, but the Warden disagreed.
As a punishment, Cassian and Wren had to clean lamp tunnels.
The first evening, they scrubbed the lamps and did not speak.
Cassian said Wren thought she was special, and they argued.
Old Ibb brought them hot tea and a short story.
Wren showed Cassian how to listen to a lamp first.
On the fifth evening, they found lamps with no hum.
To her surprise, Cassian said that he could hear it too.
They agreed to say nothing until they knew more.
That night, the lamps in the Fifth Gallery went dark.
Warden Marrow came and sang a song to calm the students.
Wren told her friends everything and said she was sorry.
The four friends opened a big map of the galleries.
The crosses made a line, and the line led downwards.
Priya made a line of frost, and it stopped at the silence.
Cassian's strong hum helped them find the edges of each silence.
The friends kept watch at night, wrapped in warm blankets.
On the fourth night, a cloaked figure came with a glass jar.
The lamp's song flowed into the jar, and the lamp went quiet.
Priya made a small sound, and the figure ran away.
They chased the figure through the galleries and up the stairs.
The figure ran into a stone wall and was gone.
The page showed a drawing of a great crystal.
The words said that when the mountain was quiet, she would wake.
Cassian looked at the page for a long time and walked away.
The next evening, Wren found Cassian alone on a stone step.
Cassian said the writing was his uncle's, Master Hale's.
Cassian said that his parents were always far away.
Wren said they must learn the truth before blaming anyone.
Tobe said that old Ibb might know the old stories.
Old Ibb sat by his fire and began to tell a story.
Ibb said that Elin Hale went below and never came back.
On the way back, Tobe asked who the girl in the page was.
Winter came, and more lamps lost their hum.
Pike told the class about the Long Note test in spring.
In the first try, most students lasted only a few minutes.
Cassian tried hard, but his hum cracked after four minutes.
Wren thought of her father's lamp and held the note longer.
Wren helped Cassian hum softly, and he held the note longer.
Tobe counted in the cave, and the numbers made a song.
Spring came, and the mountain began to drip and sing.
The four friends promised to pass the test and find the truth.
In spring, the first years went on a trip with lanterns.
They walked a long way down, and they heard a roar.
Before them, a huge waterfall fell into a dark lake.
Each student sent a note into the singing water.
Master Hale stood alone, looking into the water.
Wren heard a thin gap in the song of the Falls.
Wren told her friends, and Tobe tried to remember something.
Tobe counted the nights and found that cuts came every ninth night.
The next ninth night was Thursday, only three days away.
Pike gave them a bell and told them to watch carefully.
On Wednesday, the friends made a careful plan for Thursday.
In Stone class, Hale told Cassian to take good care.
That night, the four friends hid in the Eighth Gallery.
They waited a long time, and Tobe counted the hours.
At midnight, a deep bell rang, and they sat very still.
A cloaked man came up the stair, carrying a basket.
The hood fell back, and it was Master Hale.
Hale held a jar to a lamp and whispered to himself.
Cassian rang the brass bell, and its sound rang out.
Hale heard the bell and hurried down the Ninth Stair.
A rusty chain hung across the top of the Ninth Stair.
Wren listened, and the mountain seemed to say go down.
The four friends stepped over the chain and went down.
The stair wound down, and the hum became deeper and slower.
The steps were wet, so Priya made frost to help them grip.
On the wall, they found words scratched into the stone.
Tobe's counting came back from below, and Wren heard footsteps stop.
At the bottom, they saw a huge black door, and Hale.
Hale told the children why he had taken the hum.
Hale touched the door, and it slowly swung open.
Behind the door was a huge cave with a great crystal.
Hale put his basket down, and the jars began to glow.
Wren put her ear against the great crystal and listened.
Wren understood that the hum went round in a great circle.
Wren told Hale what she had heard, and he shook his head.
Deep in the stone, Wren heard a girl's quiet voice.
Wren told Hale what Elin's echo had said.
Hale wept, and Cassian took his hand and held it.
Hale opened the jars, and the lights flowed to the crystal.
The four friends and Hale sang together to the crystal.
The bell woke the school, and many people came running.
The Warden raised her hand, and everyone stood still.
One by one, the teachers and students joined the song.
The song grew louder, and the crystal began to blaze.
A girl made of light rose out of the crystal.
The girl spoke to her father in a warm, clear voice.
Hale said her name, and she smiled at him gently.
Then the girl faded gently into the light of the crystal.
The mountain's hum was whole again, deep and strong.
All across the Academy, the lamps blazed again.
At the top of the stair, old Ibb was waiting with tea.
Hale told Warden Marrow the whole truth about the jars.
Warden Marrow did not send Hale away from the Academy.
The Warden made a new rule: the whole school would sing every spring.
The whole school sang together under thousands of glowing lamps.
Cassian said sorry to Wren, and they became friends.
Hale played chess with Cassian, and he smiled again.
The four friends studied together and laughed a great deal.
On test day, the first years sat in the Quiet Room.
Wren held the Long Note for a whole hour.
Her friends passed the test too, and the school had a feast.
Priya and Tobe gave Wren small presents before they left.
Wren said goodbye to old Ibb in the stable cave.
Cassian gave Wren a map he had drawn himself.
Pike gave Wren a small lantern of her own.
The Great Door opened at once, and she rode out.
She rode down the mountain for three long days.
In the village, Dill Hobbs asked her about the mountain.
Wren ran to her father and hugged him tightly.
Wren lit the first lamp and heard the mountain's hum.
B1B2: Wren Tallow stands in the village lane at dusk, her ear pressed against a glowing lamp. Inside the flame she can hear a faint hum, as soft and steady as a sleeping cat.
Every evening Wren follows her father Alder on his round, carrying the taper while he climbs the ladder. She is sure the lamps hum a little louder when she stands beneath them.
When Wren rests her palm on the old wall beside the well, she feels another hum entirely. It is far slower than the song of a flame, deep and slow like a great animal asleep.
A group of village children passes by, led by a loud boy called Dill Hobbs. They laugh at Wren for pressing her ear to a wall and call her Wall-Ear.
By the fire that night, Wren asks her father whether there is something wrong with her. Alder shakes his head slowly and says that his own grandmother used to say the lamps sang to her, too.
On a still autumn night, Wren hears something new. Every lamp in the village hums in the same direction, as if leaning towards the black shape of Orrenfell far to the north.
Unable to sleep, Wren opens her attic window and presses her ear to the cold sill. Far away the mountain is humming, but its song is thin and strained, like a thread pulled too tight.
At dawn the next morning, a tall, thin stranger walks into the lane carrying a lantern. Wren notices at once that it glows steadily although it has no flame and no oil.
The stranger stops beside the lamp where Wren often stands and lays his ear against the post. He smiles and says that this lamp has been humming to someone for a very long time.
Alder opens the cottage door and looks the stranger up and down with some caution. The tall man introduces himself as Master Ostrander Pike and asks, very politely, if he might speak with Wren.

Master Pike sits at the kitchen table and eats his porridge slowly, as if he has all the time in the world. He explains that he teaches a subject called Listening, and that he travels the land looking for a certain kind of child.
When the porridge is finished, Pike reaches into his coat and takes out a small, plain grey stone. He holds it out to Wren and asks her, quietly, to tell him what she hears.
The moment her fingers close around it, the stone begins to hum. Wren hums softly in reply, and to her amazement the stone answers her, note for note, like a friend.

Pike unrolls a map and points to a tall peak called Orrenfell, three days' ride to the north. Inside it, he says, is the Academy Under the Mountain, where children who can hear the Hum are taught to use their gift.
Alder crosses his arms and asks every question that a careful father should ask. How far is it, who will care for her, what does it cost, and will she be allowed to come home?
Alder says that he needs some air, and walks out alone to the last lamp in the lane. Through the window Wren watches him stand there for a long time with his hand on the cold iron post.

That night, by the fire, Alder tells Wren that a gift is like a seed, and that it needs the right soil. He says that he can light the lamps alone, and that it would be wrong to keep her from a place where she belongs.

In the morning Wren packs her small bag with two dresses, a warm cloak and her mother's hairbrush. Her father presses a small brass lamp-key into her hand and tells her it is the one he used on his very first night.

News travels fast in a small village, and by the time Wren reaches the gate a crowd of neighbours has gathered. Old Mags Fenner gives her a woollen scarf, and even Dill Hobbs stands at the back without a word to say.

Wren throws her arms around her father at the gate and holds on for as long as she can. Then she climbs onto the mule beside Master Pike, and as they ride away every lamp in the village seems to hum a quiet goodbye.
Wren's mule is called Dumpling, and she is round, slow and very sure of her feet. Behind Master Pike's tall mule, Sorrel, they climb into the cool pine woods at the foot of Orrenfell.

They stop to eat bread beside a stream, and Wren notices that the water hums too, in a bright, tumbling way. Pike smiles and tells her the first rule of Listening: before you do anything else, you must listen.

That night they camp under the pines, and Pike's lantern gives off a soft light although it holds no oil. He explains that the Hum lives in all things, and that a good listener can learn to hold it and even to lend it.
On the second morning Pike asks Wren to stand still and listen with her feet. Soon she can feel a slow, deep hum rising through the soles of her boots, as if the mountain itself were breathing.
Above the trees the land is bare, grey and windy, and a hawk circles slowly overhead. To her delight Wren can hear its hum, small and fierce, and also the faint song of the grass between the stones.

At sunset they reach Crow's Rest, a low stone hut on a ledge, where old Nan Crowe keeps a flock of goats. She welcomes them in, gives them warm milk, and says that Pike is the only visitor she has had all year.

Late that night, Wren lies in her blanket pretending to sleep, and she hears Nan and Pike talking in low voices. Nan says that the mountain's songs have been growing thin, and Pike asks her, gently, not to say so in front of the child.
On the third morning the path climbs into a country of grey cliffs, and the clouds hang lower than their heads. Wren wraps Mags Fenner's scarf around her neck and is glad of it.

Wren admits to Pike that she is afraid the Academy will send her home, because she is only a lamplighter's daughter. He tells her that nobody is chosen for their family, and that the Great Door listens only for a true hum.
Suddenly the clouds tear open, and there in the cliff stands a door of grey stone, three times taller than a house. It is carved all over with tiny lamps, and it is closed and perfectly silent.

Wren puts her hands on the stone and pushes, but the Great Door does not move even a little. Pike tells her kindly that doors like this one cannot be pushed or pulled, only asked, and he steps back to let her try.

Wren hums at the door as clearly as she can, and then a little louder, but the stone stays dark and still. She is about to give up when she remembers the first rule of Listening, and she closes her mouth.
Wren lays her palm on the stone and listens, and slowly she hears it, a deep, shy note hidden inside the door itself. She hums softly to match it, and one by one the carved lamps begin to glow.

With a long, low rumble, the Great Door swings open, wide enough for a cart and horse. Warm golden light spills out across the wet stones, and a smell of woodsmoke and old books drifts out into the cold air.
Just inside the door an old man with a broom comes shuffling out of a stable cave to take the mules. This is Ibb, the caretaker, and he says that the door has not opened so quickly in years.

The tunnel's walls glow with soft green moss, and it ends suddenly on a high stone ledge. Below it a whole city lies inside the mountain, with thousands of lamps among stone towers and arching bridges.

As they cross a long stone bridge, Pike points down into the darkness far beneath them. He tells Wren that at the very heart of the mountain lies the Heartstone, a great crystal whose hum gives the whole Academy its light.
Pike leaves Wren in the Hall of Lamps, a huge round room hung with a thousand lanterns. About thirty other new students are already there, from all over the land, and every one of them looks nervous.

A tall woman in a long grey gown walks to the front of the hall, and every whisper stops at once. This is Warden Isolde Marrow, head of the Academy, and when she speaks, her voice rings out like a bell.
The Warden raises three fingers and tells them the rules of the Academy. Listen first, never go below the Ninth Stair, and always give back what you borrow.
After the Warden's speech, an older student leads the new children up a long, winding stair, past gallery after gallery. Wren counts six levels before they step out into a wide, curving hall.
Wren's name is painted on a round door halfway along the gallery. Inside is a round, cosy room with three beds, three wooden chests and a wide window full of softly glowing moss.
A dark-haired girl is already sitting on the bed by the window with her arms folded. She says her name is Priya Anand, that this bed is hers, and that nobody is to touch her blue blanket.

Priya tells her that she has come all the way from Velmara, a city of canals so far away that the journey took twenty days. As if to prove she belongs, she hums, and a patch of frost on the floor melts away.
A round-faced boy bumps through the door dragging a heavy trunk, with a loaf of bread tucked under one arm. He says he is Tobias Kettle, a baker's son from Lowmarket, but everybody calls him Tobe.

The three roommates sit on the rug and share Tobe's bread, which is still a little warm. When Wren says that she is only a lamplighter's daughter, Priya says it is the best thing she has heard all day.

That night the moss on the window dims to a gentle, sleepy glow, and Wren feels a sharp pang of homesickness. In the dark, Tobe begins to count out loud, very slowly, because he says numbers help him sleep.
At breakfast, a tall, proud boy called Cassian Vale looks across the long table at Wren's village boots and gives a little sneer. His own boots are polished so well that they shine like water.
Priya puts down her spoon and tells Cassian that he looks like a pigeon in a nice coat. As she speaks, a thin skin of frost creeps across his bowl, until Tobe gives her sleeve a nervous tug.

Outside the dining hall a long timetable is pinned to the wall, listing lessons with strange and wonderful names. Wren runs her finger down it and finds that the very first class of the day is Listening, with Master Pike.

The Quiet Room is a round chamber with grey walls and a high, domed ceiling, and no sound from the Academy seems to reach it. The new students sit on cushions in a ring while Master Pike's lantern glows in the middle.
Pike walks around the ring and places a smooth pebble in every student's hand. The first task, he says, is simple: sit in silence, and find the hum of the pebble.
The minutes drag on, and the silence grows longer and heavier. Priya scratches her nose, a boy at the back sighs loudly, and Tobe's stomach rumbles so loudly that three students giggle.
Wren shuts her eyes and holds the pebble in her open palm, as she once held the stone in the village lane. Very soon she hears it, a small, round, gentle hum like a bee asleep in a flower.
Across the ring, Cassian frowns ferociously at his pebble. His hum is strong, but harsh, and the poor pebble buzzes and shivers until it jumps off his knee and rolls noisily across the floor.

Pike returns the pebble and says that a strong hum is fine, but a hammer is for building, not for listening. Cassian mutters under his breath and shoots a look at Wren, as if the whole thing were her fault.

In Echo class, Mistress Odalys Brook, a cheerful woman with grey curls, tells the students to send a hum into a deep, dark cave. When Tobe's turn comes, he stands frozen with his hands over his ears, and whispers that he is afraid of what might come back.
Wren takes Tobe's hand and suggests that he hum his counting instead, since numbers never frighten him. He tries, and the cave sings his numbers back in a ringing chain, until he laughs out loud.
In Tuning class Priya's quick, bright hum calms a sheet of frost across the floor, and Pike looks very pleased. He shows the class how every stone can be tuned, a little like a string on a fiddle.

That evening the three friends kneel on the patchwork rug and tune pebbles until they are all humming the same note. Afterwards Wren writes her first letter to her father, and tells him that she is happier than she has ever been.

Stone class is taught by Master Corvin Hale, a thin, grey-haired man with a quiet voice and tired eyes. Cassian, who is his nephew, sits very straight in the front row, but his uncle hardly seems to see him.
Hale lays his palm flat against the wall and tells the class that stones remember every song ever sung near them. His voice breaks a little on the last word, and nobody in the room dares to move.

One afternoon, Wren follows a stair she has never noticed and finds herself in the Hall of Held Breath. Tall shelves rise into the dark above her, and all around her she can hear a soft, rustling whisper.

At first the whispers are only noise, but when Wren sits quite still in a deep chair, one book begins to speak clearly. It is a thin blue volume, and it tells her the story of how the very first lamp was lit.

After that Wren spends every free hour in the Hall, and soon she reads about the Heartstone. The old books say that its hum travels in a great circle through the mountain, from the crystal to every lamp and back again.

Priya and Tobe track Wren down among the shelves, and Tobe is carrying a small green book that whispers number puzzles. Priya says that she cannot sit still long enough to hear a single word, which makes the other two laugh.

Old Ibb is sweeping the floor of the Hall, and he has heard every word they have said. When Wren asks him a question about the lowest stair, he leans on his broom and says that some questions keep until the right time.

Once a week a cart brings post to the Great Door, and on Friday there is a letter for Wren in her father's careful handwriting. He writes that he has lit every lamp by himself, and that even Dill Hobbs has asked after her.
One evening Wren notices Cassian sitting alone at a far table, hunched over a heavy book. He looks lonely, but when he sees her watching, he snaps the book shut and strides away.
Late that night, as Wren leaves the Hall, every book on every shelf stops whispering at the same moment. The silence is so sudden and complete that she feels a cold shiver run down her back.
Wren hurries back to the Sixth Gallery, where the lamps are humming as sweetly as ever. Halfway along the hall she slows down, because one stretch of floor feels strangely cold beneath her boots.
Wren kneels and presses her ear against the floor, and under the stone she hears the slow hum of the mountain. In one place there is a gap, like a hole in a piece of cloth.
Once she has heard the silence, Wren cannot stop hearing it. In Tuning class the next morning she senses thin places in the hum, like missing stitches in a sock, and her stone will not answer.
When the others have left, Pike asks Wren to stay behind and leads her up a narrow stair. His small office is crowded with lanterns of every shape, all humming softly together like a choir at rest.
Pike listens to everything Wren tells him, and then he admits that he has been worried too. The Heartstone has been growing quiet for many months, he says, and he begs her to say nothing for now.

Pike gives her a small notebook and tells her to write down every silence she finds, with the place and the hour. Listening, he says, is not only about hearing, but also about paying careful attention.
Keeping a secret from her friends is harder than Wren expected. When Priya asks why she keeps staring at the floor, she says she is only homesick, and she dislikes herself a little for the lie.
In Stone class, Master Hale looks thinner and more tired than ever, with dark shadows under his eyes. When a lamp flickers over his desk, he stares at it in alarm and hurries out of the room.
In a corridor, Cassian challenges Wren to a hum contest, saying that he wants to find out who is the best listener in their year. Wren politely says no, which seems to make him even angrier.

One morning the first snow of winter drifts down through the Skylight Shaft, a narrow chimney of rock far above the great cavern. Every student is talking about Lantern Night, which is only three weeks away.
In the weeks before midwinter, every student polishes a small brass lamp in the workshop cave. On Lantern Night each of them must light their lamp using nothing but their own hum.

Night after night the three friends practise on the rug, but none of the lamps will light, and they only make a few little sparks. Priya's sparks are silver, Tobe's are gold, and Wren's are a strange, bright blue.

On Lantern Night the Hall of Lamps is dark, and snow drifts down through the Skylight Shaft onto the students' hair. Warden Marrow stands in the middle with one candle and says that each student will lend the mountain a light.
The students go up one at a time, and Priya is among the first. She hums one quick, clear note, and her lamp bursts into a pale silver flame that sparkles like frost, and the whole hall applauds.
Tobe goes up next, pale as flour, and counts under his breath as he hums. His lamp glows with a steady golden flame, and he stares at it as if it were a miracle.
Wren steps up to the table, shuts her eyes, and listens to the lamp before she hums to it. The wick blazes with a clear, bright blue flame, and the hall falls completely silent.

The Warden's eyes widen as she stares at the blue flame, and she looks at Pike, who has gone very still. Wren cannot tell whether he is glad or frightened, and she has a sinking feeling that it might be both.
Cassian steps forward with his chin high and hums as loudly as he can, but his lamp only sputters and goes out. He tries again with even more force, and the second time the wick does not even catch.
Cassian turns on Wren in front of everyone and says she hummed over him and spoiled his lamp. The Warden calmly replies that nobody can take another person's hum just by listening to it.
The Warden says that a quarrel on Lantern Night is not a good beginning, and she gives them a task. For a week, Cassian and Wren must clean the lamp tunnels together every evening.
The lamp tunnels run behind every gallery, low and narrow, and the lamps inside them are black with soot. On the first evening, Wren and Cassian scrub side by side and do not say a single word.

By the second evening Cassian cannot keep quiet any longer, and he says that Wren thinks she is special. She answers that she only listens, and the argument echoes up and down the tunnel until both are red-faced.
Old Ibb appears at the mouth of the tunnel with a pot of hot tea and two chipped cups. He says that soot is the breath of the mountain, and that these tunnels have long memories and short patience.
On the third evening, Wren shows Cassian how to listen to a lamp before he cleans it. He tries it, very reluctantly, and the soot lifts off the glass far more easily than before.
On the fifth evening Wren stops and holds up her hand. Along one stretch of the tunnel every lamp is lit, but not one of them hums, and the light has a flat, empty look.
To Wren's astonishment, Cassian lays his hand on one of the silent lamps and goes pale. In a low voice he says that he can feel it too, and that it is not a natural silence.
Wren and Cassian agree to say nothing until they understand more. Cassian mentions, almost to himself, that his uncle has hardly slept since the autumn and that he is not sure why.
That night, in the small hours, the lamps of the Fifth Gallery fail one by one, and even the glowing moss fades. The students wake in the cold and the dark, and somebody begins to cry.
Warden Marrow hurries in with a single candle, and she does not scold or explain. Instead she begins to sing, in a clear voice like a bell, and one by one the frightened students grow calm.

Afterwards, when the lamps flicker back, Wren tells Priya and Tobe about the silences and says she is sorry for lying. Priya forgives her, and Cassian, who has been listening nearby, quietly asks if he can join them.

In the quiet corner of the Hall of Held Breath, the four friends spread a large map of the Academy on the floor. Tobe takes out a stub of chalk and marks every silence from Wren's notebook with a small cross.
When all the crosses are marked, a pattern appears that nobody expected. The silences are not scattered at random, because they lead, gallery by gallery, steadily down toward the Ninth Stair.

Priya has an idea, and one night she draws a thin line of frost across the gallery floor with a hum. The line runs smoothly until it reaches a silent patch, and there it stops dead, as if it has hit a wall.
Cassian proves useful after all, because his strong, heavy hum can feel the edges of a silence like a bruise. For the first time, the friends begin to treat him as one of them.

They decide to watch the Fifth Gallery at night, in case somebody comes to make a silence. Wrapped in blankets and sharing Tobe's bread, they take turns to stay awake while the dark creeps around them.
On the fourth night, just after midnight, a cloaked figure walks silently along the gallery with a glass jar cradled in both hands. It stops beside a lamp, lifts the jar and holds it close.
A thread of pale light curls out of the flame and into the jar, and the lamp's hum fades to nothing. The figure screws a lid onto the jar and the whole gallery feels colder at once.
Priya's foot slips on a patch of her own frost, and she gasps out loud. The cloaked figure whips around, hesitates for a heartbeat, and then runs off into the dark with the jar held tight.
The chase takes them through galleries, down stairs and along narrow bridges, with Tobe counting every turn under his breath. Cassian shouts for the figure to stop, but it only runs faster.
The figure runs straight at a blank stone wall at the end of a gallery and simply vanishes into it. By the time the friends arrive, there is only the wall, and a folded page lying on the floor.
Wren unfolds the page in the light of Tobe's lantern. It shows a careful drawing of a great crystal at the end of a spiral stair, with a few lines of neat writing beneath it.
Under the drawing, a few small words say that when the mountain is quiet, she will wake. Cassian leans over, looks at the neat handwriting, and goes as pale as milk.
Cassian takes the page, studies the writing for a long moment, and then walks quickly away without a word. That night Wren lies awake, staring at the glowing moss, and wonders what he knows.
The next evening Wren finds Cassian sitting alone on a quiet stone stair, with a small lamp beside him and the page in his lap. She says nothing, and quietly sits down beside him on the cold step.
Cassian tells her in a flat voice that the handwriting is his uncle's. He knows it well, he says, because Master Hale has written to him every month since he was six years old.

Cassian explains that his parents are mapmakers who are always travelling, and that he has spent most summers here with his uncle. Master Hale was once warm and funny, he says, and then something changed.
Wren tells Cassian that they must find out the truth before they blame anyone, and he nods slowly. He asks her not to tell the teachers yet, and she says she will not say a word until they know more.
Back in the round room, Cassian tells Priya and Tobe what he has told Wren. Tobe thinks for a long minute, and suggests that they ask Ibb, who knows every old story in the mountain.

In his warm stable cave, with Dumpling and Sorrel munching hay nearby, Ibb pokes the fire and puts a kettle on. Then, with the four children on upturned buckets, he begins to tell them about a girl named Elin Hale.
