Thirty years ago, Ibb says, Master Hale's daughter Elin was the best listener of her year. One night she went below the Ninth Stair to hear the Heartstone sing, and she was never seen again; only her echo remains.
Walking back from Ibb's cave, Tobe wonders aloud who the she in the page might be. Cassian says very quietly that it must be Elin, and that his uncle must hope that something will wake her.
Winter deepens outside, and more lamps lose their hum in other galleries, though the cloaked figure does not return to the Fifth. Tobe marks every new cross on the map in his small, tidy chalk.
One morning Pike announces that the spring test of the first year will be the Long Note. Each student must hold a single, steady hum, without a break, for one whole hour.

In their first attempts, most of the students last only a few minutes before their hum wobbles and stops. Priya sneezes at the third minute, and Tobe keeps going the longest by counting silently behind his hum.
Cassian goes at the Long Note with all his strength, and his hum cracks after four minutes. Pike tells him gently that this test is not about strength, but about being as soft and patient as grass.
Wren discovers a trick of her own, which is to imagine the slow breathing of her father's lamp in the village lane. She holds her note for twenty minutes before her throat gets tired.
In the lamp tunnels, where they used to scrub, Wren helps Cassian to practise a softer, rounder hum. After many failures he holds a note for ten whole minutes, and his eyes shine with surprise.
In Echo class, Mistress Brook shows Tobe how to turn his counting into a single long song. He loses himself in the numbers, and holds the note for half an hour without noticing.
The first thaw comes, and the whole mountain fills with the sound of dripping water. A letter arrives from Alder, and inside is a pressed snowdrop from the lane at Hollin Ford.

That night the four friends sit in a circle on the patchwork rug, with their hands joined. They promise each other that they will all hold the Long Note for an hour, and that they will find out the truth.

In spring the first-year students are taken on a trip to the Singing Falls, an underground waterfall far below the galleries. Master Hale and Mistress Brook lead the way, and everyone carries a small lantern.
The tunnel is long and damp, and it winds steadily downward through the rock. A distant roaring grows louder with every step, until it seems to shake the very walls around them.
They step out onto a stone ledge, and there before them is the Singing Falls. A huge waterfall plunges into a dark lake far below, and the falling water sings in a hundred different voices.
Mistress Brook tells the class that water remembers every song that has ever fallen into it. Each student sends a note toward the falls, and the water carries it away and weaves it into the choir.
Master Hale does not sing with the others, but stands apart at the edge of the ledge. He stares down into the lake with a lost look, and Cassian watches him closely from a few steps away.
When the others have finished, Wren listens to the great song of the Falls, and her heart sinks. Somewhere in the middle of the choir there is a thin gap, exactly like the silences in the lamps.
Wren whispers the news to her friends behind a screen of drifting spray. Tobe frowns and looks at the sky of the cavern, as though he is trying to remember something important about the nights.
Tobe pulls out Wren's notebook and counts the dates on his fingers, whispering numbers to himself. After a long minute he looks up, and says that every silence has come on a ninth night, exactly.
Tobe counts forward, and says that the next ninth night will fall on Thursday, only three days from now. The friends look at each other, because for the first time they know exactly when to look.

Back at the Academy they tell Pike about the jars and the pattern, though Cassian keeps the page to himself. Pike looks worried, and says that the Warden is away until Friday, so they must only watch and ring his small brass bell.

On Wednesday night the four friends make their plan on the patchwork rug. Priya will bring cloaks, Tobe will bring bread, and Cassian asks in a small voice what will happen if he is wrong about his uncle.

Thursday drags by slowly, and Master Hale teaches Stone class more gently than usual, as if something heavy has been lifted from him. When the class ends, he puts a hand on Cassian's shoulder and tells him to take good care of himself.

As evening comes, the four friends creep up to the Eighth Gallery, a high stone balcony that overlooks the great stair to the lower levels. They crouch behind its stone balustrade in the shadows, and they begin to wait.

They wait for many hours in the cold, sharing Tobe's bread and whispering very little. Priya's nervous frost creeps over the rail, Tobe counts the hours, and Wren listens to the mountain's thin, trembling hum.
At midnight a deep bell tolls somewhere far below, and its note rolls slowly out across the cavern. The four friends go very still, and even Tobe stops counting.

A figure in a long cloak comes slowly up the great stair, carrying a basket that clinks softly with glass. It makes no light of its own, and it keeps close to the wall, as if it does not want to be seen.
As the figure passes beneath a lamp, its hood slips back, and the light falls on a thin, tired face. It is Master Hale, and Cassian whispers the word uncle so quietly that only Wren hears it.
Hale stops at a lamp, lifts a jar with trembling hands and draws the lamp's hum into it. They hear him murmur, very softly, that soon he will see Elin again.
Cassian takes the bell from Wren and stares at it for a long moment, torn between love and duty. At last he rings it, and its clear, bright note carries through all the galleries of the Academy.
Below them, Hale freezes at the sound, his face turned up in alarm. He snatches up his basket and hurries down toward the Ninth Stair, and the dark soon swallows his footsteps.
At the head of the Ninth Stair, an old rusty chain hangs across the opening, with a small sign beside it. The friends stop short, and all of them remember the second rule.
Wren shuts her eyes and does what she has been taught, which is to listen first. The mountain's hum is thin and desperate, and it seems to be drawing her down, as if it needs somebody to come.
One by one, the four friends climb over the chain and onto the first step. Tobe is trembling all over, but he begins to count the steps in a whisper, and that seems to help.

The stair winds down and down in a tight spiral, and the glowing moss on the walls turns from green to a deep, dark blue. The hum of the mountain grows deeper and slower, like the beat of an enormous heart.
Lower down, the steps are wet and slippery, and Cassian nearly falls. Priya hums a quick note and scatters a fine frost on each step, which grips their boots like sand.
Halfway down, Wren's lantern shows words scratched into the stone wall, very small and a little crooked. They say, Elin Hale was here, aged fifteen, and Cassian stares at them without a sound.
Tobe counts out loud, and the echo of his voice comes back from below much sooner than before. Wren tells them that the bottom is near, because the footsteps of Master Hale have stopped.

At the bottom of the stair stands a great arched door of black stone, traced with fine silver lines. Master Hale is standing in front of it with his back to them, and his basket of jars sits at his feet.
Hale turns, and he is not angry, only very tired. He says that the Heartstone's song hides his daughter's echo, and that he hoped silence would let her wake.
Hale lays his palm against the black door, and the silver lines flare into light. Slowly, without a sound, the door swings open, and a pale glow spills out of the great chamber beyond.
Behind the door lies the Hollow, a vast domed chamber carved from the living rock. In the middle stands the Heartstone, a crystal as big as a house, and it is glowing faintly and unsteadily.
Hale walks slowly across the floor and sets his basket down at the foot of the great crystal. The jars inside begin to glow and whisper, as though they know exactly where they are.
Wren crosses the floor, step by careful step, and lays her ear against the cool surface of the Heartstone. Inside the crystal, a pale light moves slowly, round and round, like a fish in a deep pool.
Slowly, as the great hum rolls through her, Wren understands what she is hearing. The hum travels in a great circle from the Heartstone to every lamp and back, and Hale's jars have cut it.
Wren turns to Hale and tells him gently what she has heard. He shakes his head and says that he only wanted to borrow a little hum, and never meant to keep it.
Wren leans against the crystal again and listens deeper than she has ever listened. Far below the great hum she hears a girl's voice, only an echo, saying clearly that the song must go home.
Wren turns to Hale and repeats the words exactly as she heard them. For a long time he stands like a statue, and his face goes through a hundred changes in the pale light.

Hale sinks to his knees in front of the Heartstone, and weeps like a child. Cassian kneels beside him and takes his hand, and tells him in a steady voice that it is time to give back what he borrowed.
With shaking fingers, Hale unscrews the jars one after another. The stolen hum rises from each in a thread of silver light, and the threads flow like little rivers toward the Heartstone.
Wren, Priya, Tobe and Cassian each lend their own hum to the song, silver and gold and blue and strong. Hale lifts his head and joins them, and together they sing to the Heartstone.

The bell has woken the whole Academy, and Master Pike comes running down the Ninth Stair. Warden Marrow, who has returned early from the mountain, is with him, and a crowd of teachers and students follows behind.
At the door of the Hollow they stop in astonishment, for the sight before them is like nothing that they have ever seen. The Warden raises her hand, and every voice behind her falls silent.
One by one, the newcomers understand what they are hearing and begin to sing. Pike's deep voice joins first, then Mistress Brook, and Ibb's dry old rasp, and soon the whole Hollow is full of voices.
The song grows louder and fuller, until it seems to shake the very stone of the chamber. The Heartstone begins to blaze, and its light turns from pale grey to gold to a dazzling white.

In the heart of the blazing crystal, a shape begins to rise like mist from a lake. It is a girl of fifteen made of soft golden light, and everyone in the Hollow knows without being told that it is Elin's echo.
Elin's echo looks at her father with kind eyes and speaks in a warm, clear voice. She tells him that she was never lost, only listening, and she thanks him for loving her so well for so long.
Hale whispers her name, and she smiles at him, and then at Cassian, who is holding his uncle's hand. She asks her father to teach the song to others, as he once taught it to her.

Elin's echo turns to the children, thanks them, and then fades slowly into the golden light of the Heartstone. She goes like the last note of a song, so softly that nobody can say exactly when she is gone.

The circle has closed, and the great hum of the Heartstone is whole again, deep and steady and warm. Wren puts her palm against the crystal, and she can feel the mountain's gratitude flowing up her arm.
Across the whole Academy, the lamps flare up again at once, from the lowest tunnel to the highest gallery. The moss glows green on every wall, and the cold slowly lifts from every hall and stair.

The whole company climbs the Ninth Stair together, tired and happy, with Hale walking between Cassian and Pike. At the top, Ibb is waiting with his broom and a huge pot of tea, and he says it took them long enough.

In her lamplit study, Hale stands before Warden Marrow with his head bowed, and tells her the whole truth. The four children stand beside him and add their own part, including the chain they climbed over.

To everyone's surprise, the Warden does not send Hale away, but gives him the care of the Heartstone. She tells the children that their courage was good, but that a rule is never a thing to break lightly.

At breakfast the Warden stands before the whole school and announces a new tradition. Every spring, she says, the entire Academy will gather and sing to the mountain, so that it always gives back what it takes.
At the first Giving Back, the whole school gathers beneath the thousand lamps of the great hall and sings together. The lamps hum along, and the mountain seems to sing back from every wall.
A few days later Cassian finds Wren on a high bridge and says that he is sorry for laughing at her boots. He also thanks her for helping his uncle, and from that day on the two are friends.

Master Hale begins to smile again, and in the evenings he plays chess with Cassian beside the glowing Heartstone. His Stone class changes too, and the students say that his voice has found its colour.
In the weeks before the test the four friends are never apart. Tobe draws a map of every lamp in the Academy, and Priya freezes a small pool by the Falls so they can slide on it.
On the day of the Long Note test, the first years sit in rows in the Quiet Room, nervous and silent. Pike tells them that the hour is not a race, because it is a gift of patience to the mountain.

Wren thinks of her father's lamp in the lane, slow and steady, and the hum flows out of her as easily as breathing. When the hourglass runs out, she is still humming, and Pike's eyes shine as he nods.

Priya, Tobe and Cassian all pass the Long Note as well, and Priya says that her nose behaved for the whole hour. That night the school holds a farewell feast under the thousand lamps of the great hall.

On the last evening, Priya ties a blue ribbon around Wren's wrist, and Tobe gives her a loaf that he baked himself. They promise to meet again in the autumn, and nobody manages to say goodbye without crying.
In the stable cave, Wren says goodbye to Ibb and to Dumpling, who is eating a carrot. Ibb leans on his broom and tells her that giving back is the whole of it, and the rest is only details.

Cassian gives Wren a small folded map of the Academy that he has drawn himself, with every gallery named in his neat handwriting. He tells her, a little shyly, that his uncle thanks her too, and that he will see her in autumn.
At the Great Door, on the morning she leaves, Master Pike gives Wren a small lantern of her own. It burns without oil, as his does, and its soft hum seems to fit her like a glove.
Wren hums one quiet note at the Great Door, and it swings open at once. Dumpling plods out into the bright spring sunshine, and the carved lamps on the door glow as if they were saying goodbye.
With Pike beside her, Wren rides down the mountain for three days. The mountain's hum grows fainter behind her, and ahead she begins to hear the small bright song of the lamps of home.
At the village gate Dill Hobbs stands awkwardly with his cap in his hands and says hello. He asks what the mountain is like, and when Wren tells him, he listens carefully and does not laugh.
Wren runs down the lane and throws her arms around her father, who drops his taper and laughs. She shows him her lantern, and he says that he has been sure all spring that the lamps were missing her.

As the stars come out, Wren and her father light the first lamp of the evening together. Inside the flame she hears the faint, deep hum of the mountain, and she smiles, because she knows that she will return in the autumn.
C1C2: At dusk in the village of Hollin Ford, a twelve-year-old girl called Wren Tallow stood in the lane with her ear pressed against a glowing lamp. Inside the glass, beneath the crackle of the flame, there lived a faint and steady hum, as soft as a cat asleep in the sun. It was a sound that nobody else in the village had ever noticed, and she had never found the right words to describe it.

Every evening, as the light faded from the hills, Wren followed her father Alder along the lane while he climbed his ladder and lit one lamp after another. She carried the long taper and held the ladder steady, and she could have sworn that each lamp hummed a little louder when she stood beneath it. Alder never remarked on it, but now and then he glanced down at her with a thoughtful smile.

The wall beside the village well was older than anyone could remember, and when Wren laid her palm flat against it she felt a different hum altogether. It was far slower than the song of a flame, so deep and patient that it seemed to come from the bottom of the world. She stood there for a long time, until the cold of the stone crept up her arm and the first stars came out.

A group of village children came clattering down the lane, led by a loud, freckled boy named Dill Hobbs, who stopped dead when he saw her. He nudged his friends and pointed, and soon the whole lane rang with their laughter as they chanted that Wren was Wall-Ear, who talked to bricks. Wren took her hand from the stone and walked home with her face burning and her eyes fixed firmly on the ground.

That night, sitting close to the fire with her knees drawn up, Wren asked her father in a very small voice whether something was wrong with her. Alder put down his pipe, shook his head slowly, and told her that his own grandmother had sworn all her life that the lamps sang to her, and that nobody had ever thought her strange for it. Then he smiled and said that a gift is only strange to those who have not been given it.

Late in the autumn, on a night so still that the smoke rose straight up from the chimneys, Wren heard something she had never heard before. Every lamp in the village was humming in the same direction, as though each little flame were leaning towards the great black shape of Orrenfell, which lay far away to the north beneath the stars. It was as if the whole village were listening to something that she could not quite catch.

Unable to sleep, Wren pushed open her attic window and laid her ear against the cold stone of the sill. Far away across the dark valley, the mountain was humming, but its song was thin and strained, like a thread that has been pulled so tight that it is ready to snap. She lay there until her ear grew numb, wishing that she knew what it was trying to tell her.

At dawn the next morning, a tall, thin stranger in a long grey coat walked slowly into the lane, carrying a lantern that swung gently from his hand. Wren, watching from the doorstep with a bowl of water, noticed at once that the lantern glowed with a clear and steady light, though it held neither flame nor oil. What astonished her more was that it hummed, and that its hum was the loveliest she had ever heard.

The stranger stopped beside the last lamp in the lane, the one that Wren visited more than any other, and bent to lay his ear against the iron post. He listened for a long moment with his head tilted, and then he straightened up with a smile and remarked that this lamp had clearly been humming to somebody for a very long time. Wren felt her heart begin to beat very fast, and she did not dare to move.

Alder opened the cottage door, and he looked the stranger up and down with the careful frown of a man who guards his daughter. The tall man bowed, introduced himself as Master Ostrander Pike, and asked, in a voice as kind as warm bread, whether he might speak with Alder's daughter about a matter of some importance. Halfway up the narrow stairs, Wren held her breath and waited to hear what her father would say.

Master Pike sat at the kitchen table and ate his porridge with great care, praising it twice, as though he had all the time in the world. Between mouthfuls he explained that he taught a subject called Listening at a school far to the north, and that every few years he travelled the land in search of a certain rare kind of child. Wren sat on the bottom stair with her chin on her knees, hardly daring to breathe.

When the bowl was empty, Pike reached into the pocket of his long grey coat and drew out a small stone, no bigger than a hen's egg and quite plain to look at. He held it out to Wren on the flat of his hand and asked her, in the quiet voice of a man who already knew the answer, to tell him what she heard. Wren stepped forward from the stairs, and her fingers were trembling a little as she took the stone from him.

The moment her fingers closed around the stone, it began to hum, softly at first and then with a warm and rolling note that she felt in her wrist and up her arm. Wren hummed a little in reply, almost without meaning to, and to her astonishment the stone answered her, note for note, like a friend who had been waiting years for her to speak. She had never in her life been answered before, and her eyes filled with tears.

Pike unrolled a worn map across the table and laid one long finger on a tall peak at the top of it, which was called Orrenfell. Inside that mountain, he told them, there was a school known as the Academy Under the Mountain. There, children who could hear the Hum that lives in all things were taught how to listen, how to hold the song and how to lend it to others.

Alder crossed his arms and asked every question that a careful father ought to ask, one after another, without once taking his eyes from Pike's face. How far was it, who would care for her, what would the school cost, and would she be allowed to come home again? Pike answered each one patiently and honestly, and said that the Academy asked no fee from any child who could hear, and that the road back was always open.

Alder said that he needed some air, and he went out alone to the last lamp in the lane, where he stood for a very long time with one hand resting on the cold iron post. Through the window, Wren watched him with her heart in her throat, for she had never seen him look so still or so far away. Behind her, Pike sat quietly and did not say a single word to hurry him.

That night, by the fire, Alder took his daughter's hands in his own rough ones and told her that a gift was like a seed, and that no seed could grow in soil that did not suit it. He said that he could light the village lamps perfectly well on his own, as he had done for twenty years, and that he would never forgive himself for keeping her from a place where she truly belonged. Wren buried her face in his coat and cried, and he held her until the fire burned low.

In the grey light of the morning, Wren packed her small canvas bag with two dresses, a warm cloak, a loaf of bread and the stone that Pike had said she might keep. Her father came in as she was fastening the strap and pressed into her palm a small brass lamp-key, worn smooth with use. He had carried it on his very first night as the village lamplighter, he told her, and it had never once let him down, and Wren closed her fingers around it and could not trust herself to speak.

News travels quickly in a small village, and by the time Wren reached the gate half of Hollin Ford had gathered in the lane to see her off. Old Mags Fenner pressed a thick woollen scarf into her hands, muttering that mountains were cold places. At the very back of the crowd stood Dill Hobbs with his hands in his pockets, and for once in his life he did not laugh, though a tall man in a grey coat waited beside two patient mules.

Wren threw her arms around her father at the gate and held on for as long as she dared, breathing in the smell of lamp oil and wood smoke that she knew she would never forget. Then she climbed onto the smaller of the two mules, took up the reins and rode away beside Master Pike, and she did not look back until the lane bent out of sight. Behind her, the lamps along the way were still lit, and every one of them seemed to be humming a quiet goodbye.

Wren's mule was called Dumpling, and she was round and slow and very sure of her feet, with a way of flicking her long ears whenever anybody spoke. Behind Pike's taller mule, Sorrel, they climbed steadily into the cool, resinous pine woods that lay at the foot of Orrenfell. For the first time in her life, Wren could not see the roofs of her own village.

At noon they stopped to eat bread and cheese beside a stream that tumbled noisily over mossy stones. Wren noticed that the water had a hum of its own, bright and quick and slightly changeable, like laughter in another room. Pike was delighted, and told her that this was the first rule of Listening, which was that whatever you wished to understand, you must listen to it first and speak to it afterward.

That night they made camp beneath the pines, and Pike hung his strange lantern from a low branch, where it glowed softly although it held no oil and no flame. Lying in her blanket, Wren listened while he explained that the Hum lived in every stone, every fire and every living creature. A patient listener, he said, could learn first to hear it, then to hold it, and at last to lend it to others, and she fell asleep wondering what it would feel like to lend a song.

On the second morning the pines began to thin, and Pike asked Wren to climb down from her mule and stand quite still on the stony path. He told her to listen not with her ears but with the soles of her feet, and after a moment she felt it. A slow and enormous hum was rising through her boots, as if the whole mountain were breathing in its sleep, and Pike laughed aloud at the look on her face.

Above the tree line the land became bare and grey and windy, a country of loose stones and thin grass where the mules picked their way with great caution. A hawk was circling high overhead, and to her delight Wren could hear its hum, small and fierce and bright, quite separate from the deeper song of the grass among the rocks. It struck her that the world was never silent at all, and that she had lived her whole life inside a chorus without knowing it.

At sunset they came to Crow's Rest, a low stone hut tucked into a ledge of the mountain, where a weathered old woman named Nan Crowe kept a flock of shaggy goats. She welcomed them in without a single question, gave them each a mug of warm milk, and remarked drily that Pike was the first visitor she had seen since the spring. Wren sat close to the little stove with her hands round the mug and felt the stiffness leave her legs.

Late that night, Wren lay in her blanket with her eyes tightly shut, pretending to be asleep, while Nan Crowe and Pike talked in low voices beside the stove. She heard the old woman say that the songs of the mountain had been growing thin since the summer, and that even her goats had begun to wander uneasily at night. Pike asked her very gently not to say so in front of the child, and Wren lay awake for a long time after that.

On the third morning the path climbed steeply into a country of grey cliffs, where the clouds hung so low that they drifted past the mules' ears and beaded Wren's hair with water. The cold bit through her cloak, and she wound old Mags Fenner's woollen scarf twice around her neck and was extremely grateful for it. Everything beyond a few yards had vanished into white, and the only sounds were the clatter of hooves and the slow hum of the stone.

As the afternoon wore on, Wren finally admitted what had troubled her all day, which was that the Academy would take one look at a lamplighter's daughter and send her straight home. Pike knelt in the wet stones in front of her and said that nobody was ever chosen for their family or their boots, and that the Great Door listened for only one thing. Then he asked her to hum for him, and she did, and he nodded as though that settled the matter.

Suddenly the clouds tore open like a curtain, and there, set into the very face of the cliff, stood a door of grey stone, three times taller than a house. It was carved from top to bottom with tiny lamps, thousands of them, each one no bigger than a thumbnail, and it was closed and perfectly silent. Wren slid down from her mule and stood in front of it with her heart hammering, and she knew without being told that this was the Great Door.

Wren set both hands against the carved stone and pushed with all her strength, but the Great Door did not move so much as a hair's breadth. Pike told her kindly that a door like this one could not be pushed or pulled, only asked, and that every listener who had ever entered the Academy had been obliged to ask for themselves. He stepped back among the mules and folded his arms, and Wren turned to face the great cold door entirely alone.

Wren hummed at the door as clearly and steadily as she could, and then a little louder, and then louder still, until her throat began to ache and her cheeks went hot. The stone stayed dark and cold, and the silence of it seemed to grow heavier with every breath, until she was close to tears and ready to give up entirely. Then she remembered the first rule of Listening, and she closed her mouth and stood very still.

She laid her palm flat on the cold stone and listened, and slowly, beneath her own thudding heartbeat, she began to hear a deep and shy note hidden inside the door itself. Wren did not push it or force it, but only hummed very softly in answer until the two sounds fitted together like the halves of a broken cup. All across the great stone face, the tiny carved lamps began to glow one by one, like stars coming out.

With a long, low rumble that Wren felt through the soles of her boots, the Great Door swung slowly open, wide enough to admit a loaded cart and its horse. Warm golden light spilled out across the wet stones, along with a smell of woodsmoke and old books and something sweeter that she could not name. Behind her, Master Pike gave a quiet, satisfied sigh, as though he had never doubted it for a moment.

Just inside the door, an old man with a stiff back and a very worn broom came shuffling out of a lamplit stable cave to take charge of the mules. This was Ibb, the caretaker of the Academy, who looked Wren up and down with bright, shrewd eyes and remarked that the Great Door had not opened so quickly for a new student in many years. He patted Dumpling on the nose, muttered something to her about carrots, and led both animals away.

Pike led her down a winding tunnel whose walls were covered in soft green moss, until it ended without warning on a high stone ledge, and Wren stopped so suddenly that he nearly walked into her. Below the ledge, a whole city lay hidden inside the mountain, stretching away into a cavern so vast that she could not see its farther wall, and thousands upon thousands of lamps glowed among its stone towers and arching bridges. She had thought that she knew what light was, being a lamplighter's daughter, and she had been completely wrong.

They crossed a long stone bridge with no rail, and when Wren dared to look down she saw nothing but a deep dark space glimmering faintly far below. Pike pointed into it and told her that at the very heart of the mountain lay the Heartstone, a vast crystal whose hum had lit the Academy for a thousand years. His voice was light, but she thought she heard something careful in it, like a man stepping around a hole in the floor.

Pike left her at the door of the Hall of Lamps, a huge round chamber hung with a thousand lanterns that swayed gently in the warm air. Some thirty other new students had already gathered there, from towns and farms and cities Wren had never heard of, and every one of them looked just as nervous as she felt. Nobody spoke, and the only sound was the quiet, collective humming of a roomful of lamps.

A tall woman in a long grey gown walked to the front of the hall, and every whisper died as though a door had closed on it. This was Warden Isolde Marrow, the head of the Academy, who was calm and serious and not at all unkind, and when she began to speak, her voice rang out like a great bell across the lamplit room. She welcomed them, one and all, and said that every child in the hall had been heard by the mountain.

Then the Warden raised three fingers, and the whole hall held its breath, for it was clear that this was the part that mattered most. The first rule, she said, was to listen first, the second was never to go below the Ninth Stair, and the third was to give back whatever one borrowed, whether it was a book, a favour or a song. Wren held all three rules in her mind, and the second one prickled strangely, like a splinter.

When the Warden had finished, an older student with a lantern on a pole led the new children up a long, winding stair, past gallery after gallery of carved doors and humming lamps. Wren counted six levels before they stepped out into a wide hall that curved away into the glow, its walls pierced with round wooden doors. A small brass plate beside the nearest door said that this was the Sixth Gallery.

Her name had been painted in small neat letters on a round door halfway along the gallery, and when she pushed it open she found a round, cosy room. It held three beds, three wooden chests and a deep window overgrown with softly glowing moss, and a patchwork rug lay on the floor, while a small stove ticked quietly in the corner. It was the first room that Wren had ever had entirely to herself, or very nearly.

A dark-haired girl was already sitting on the bed beside the window with her arms folded and her chin raised, as if she expected a fight. She announced that her name was Priya Anand, that this bed was hers because she had arrived first, and that nobody was to touch her blue blanket under any circumstances. Wren said that she did not want the bed by the window, and Priya blinked, looking a little disappointed.

Priya, it turned out, had come all the way from Velmara, a city of canals and bridges so far away that her journey had taken twenty days by boat, cart and train. A thin patch of frost had crept in under the door from the cold gallery, and without even looking at it she hummed one quick, clear note, and it melted away into a puddle on the stone. She glanced sideways at Wren, with a small, careful face, to see whether she was impressed.

A round-faced boy bumped through the doorway dragging a trunk that was far too heavy for him, with a loaf of bread tucked firmly under one arm like a treasure. He said breathlessly that his name was Tobias Kettle, that he was a baker's son from the town of Lowmarket, and that everyone called him Tobe, though he could not think why. He had counted the steps on the way up, he added, and there were four hundred and twelve.

The three of them sat down on the patchwork rug and shared Tobe's loaf, which was a day old but still sweet, passing it back and forth between them. When Wren confessed, rather shyly, that she was only a lamplighter's daughter from a village nobody had heard of, Priya declared that it was the best thing she had heard all day. Tobe nodded so hard that crumbs fell from his chin, and he said that he thought so too.

That night the moss in the window dimmed to a gentle, sleepy glow, and the whole mountain seemed to settle around them with a slow, deep sigh. Wren lay awake with a sharp pang of homesickness, thinking of her father walking the lane alone, until Tobe began to count out loud in the dark, very slowly, because he said numbers helped him sleep. Somewhere around three hundred, Priya, who had been pretending to be asleep all along, joined in, and a little later so did Wren.

On the first morning, at breakfast, a tall, proud boy called Cassian Vale looked down the long table at Wren's village boots, which were still caked in mud from the mountain, and gave a small, scornful laugh. His own clothes were fine, and his own boots shone like water in the lamplight. Wren felt her face go hot, though she kept her eyes on her bowl and said nothing at all.

Priya put down her spoon, looked Cassian straight in the eye, and said that he looked like a pigeon in a very nice coat. As she spoke, a thin skin of frost began to creep across the surface of his porridge, crackling softly, until Tobe gave her sleeve a nervous tug and she stopped. Cassian stared at his bowl, then at Priya, and went pink to the tips of his ears, but he did not say another word.

Outside the dining hall, a long timetable had been pinned to the wall, listing lessons with strange and wonderful names such as Echo, Stone, Tuning and Giving, which Wren read with growing excitement. Her finger travelled down the page until it stopped at the first class of the morning, which was Listening, with Master Pike, in a room called the Quiet Room. She turned to her friends, and all three of them grinned at the same moment.

The Quiet Room was a round chamber with grey walls and a high, domed ceiling, built in such a way that no sound from the rest of the Academy seemed able to reach it. The new students sat on cushions in a wide ring, shifting and whispering, while at the centre Master Pike's strange lantern glowed like a small, patient sun. Wren noticed that her ears felt oddly empty, as though she had taken off a heavy hat.

Pike walked slowly around the ring and placed a smooth grey pebble in every outstretched hand, pausing now and then to straighten someone's back. The first task, he told them, was a very simple one, which was to sit in complete silence and find the hum of the pebble, and nothing else. He did not say how long it would take, and Wren had a feeling that this was deliberate.

The minutes crawled by, and the silence grew longer and heavier until it seemed to press on the top of Wren's head. Priya scratched her nose, a boy at the back sighed loudly, and Tobe's stomach gave such an enormous rumble that three students began to giggle and one of them had to be glared at. Master Pike sat quite still in the middle of it all, with his eyes closed and a faint smile on his face.

Wren closed her eyes and let the pebble rest in her open palm, as she had so often held her ear against the village lamps. It took her a very short time to find it, a small, round and gentle hum, like a bee asleep in the heart of a flower. She hummed back so softly that nobody could possibly have heard her, and the pebble grew faintly warm in her hand.

Across the ring, Cassian scowled ferociously at his pebble, jaw clenched, humming at it as though he were trying to hammer a nail into a plank. His hum was strong, there was no doubt of that, but it was harsh and loud, and the poor pebble buzzed and shivered until it leaped off his knee and rolled noisily across the stone floor. Somebody snorted with laughter from the back of the room, and Cassian went scarlet from his collar to his hair.

Pike calmly picked up the runaway pebble and returned it to Cassian with a quiet word, saying that a strong hum was a fine thing to have, but that a hammer was made for building and not for listening. Cassian took it with a stiff nod and muttered something under his breath, and then he shot a glare at Wren across the ring, as though the whole humiliating business were somehow her fault. In that moment, Wren understood that she had made an enemy without lifting a finger.

In Echo class, Mistress Odalys Brook, a cheerful woman with a cloud of grey curls and silver earrings that chimed when she moved, told the students to send a hum into a deep cave and listen to it come back. One by one they did so, until the turn came to Tobe, who stood frozen at the mouth of the darkness with both hands pressed over his ears. He whispered, in a voice almost too small to hear, that he was afraid of what might come back, and it was Wren who stepped forward first.

Wren took Tobe's trembling hand in her own and suggested, quietly, that he should not send a hum at all, but should simply count into the cave, the way he did at night. He tried it, one, two, three, in a small shaky voice, and the cave sang the numbers back to him in a ringing, rolling chain, each one a little more beautiful than the last. By the time they reached forty, Tobe was laughing aloud, and his hands had left his ears.

In Tuning class, Priya's quick, bright hum sent a sheet of white frost shrinking back across the stone floor like a tide going out, and Pike looked quite delighted. He showed the class that every stone had a note of its own and could be nudged, very gently, toward a different one, a little like tightening the string of a fiddle. Cassian's attempt, in the corner, only sent a small crack running across his own slab, and he pretended not to notice.

That evening, the three friends knelt on the patchwork rug with a heap of pebbles between them and tuned them one by one, laughing whenever somebody got it wrong, until the whole heap was humming the same note. Afterwards, with her tongue between her teeth, Wren wrote her first letter to her father by the light of the mossy window, telling him about the pebbles, the cave and the bread. She ended it by saying that she was happier than she had ever been, and that she missed her father very much indeed.

Stone class was taught by Master Corvin Hale, a thin, grey-haired man with a very quiet voice and eyes that seemed to be looking at something a long way behind the students. Cassian, who was his nephew, sat very straight in the front row and waited for a word of praise, but his uncle only nodded at him as he might at a stranger. Wren felt a small, unwelcome twinge of pity for the proud boy in the front row.

Hale laid his palm flat against the wall and told the class, in his low, careful voice, that stones remembered every song that had ever been sung near them, and would go on remembering long after the singers had gone. His voice cracked on the last word, and for a moment he stood quite still with his eyes shut, while nobody in the room dared to stir. Then he cleared his throat and asked them, briskly, to turn to the first exercise.

One afternoon, following a staircase that she had never noticed before, Wren found herself in the Hall of Held Breath, the great library of the Academy. Shelves rose into the shadows above her head, so high that the top ones were lost in the dark, and from every direction came a soft, rustling whisper like leaves in a faraway wood. She stood in the doorway with her mouth slightly open, hardly believing that such a place could exist.

At first the whispers were only noise, a hundred tiny voices speaking all at once, but when Wren sat down in a deep chair and became completely still, one of them slowly rose above the others. It came from a thin blue book on the nearest shelf, and it told her, in a voice like a very old grandmother, the story of how the very first lamp was lit. She listened to every word without moving, and when it had finished, she found that an hour had slipped away.

After that, Wren spent every free hour in the Hall, drifting between the tall cases, and before long she found the old books that told of the Heartstone. They said that its hum travelled in a great circle through the mountain, from the crystal to every lamp and then back again to the crystal, and that for a thousand years the circle had never been broken. She read the line twice, and for some reason it gave her a shiver.

One evening, Priya and Tobe tracked Wren down among the shelves, and Tobe was carrying a small green book that whispered number puzzles to him in a happy, singsong voice. Priya declared that she had sat as still as a stone for a full minute and heard absolutely nothing. Both of her friends laughed so loudly that a nearby book stopped whispering in a huff, and a voice from the shadows hissed at them to be quiet.

Old Ibb was sweeping the floor of the Hall with long, slow strokes, and it was perfectly clear that he had heard every word they had said. When Wren asked him, as carelessly as she could, why nobody was allowed to go below the Ninth Stair, he leaned on his broom and said that some questions kept very well until the right time. His bright eyes rested on her for a moment longer than was comfortable, and then he went back to his sweeping.

Once a week a cart brought the post up the mountain to the Great Door, and on a Friday in late autumn there was a letter for Wren in her father's careful handwriting. He wrote that he had lit every lamp in Hollin Ford by himself, that the lamps hummed as steadily as ever, and that even Dill Hobbs had asked after her, though in a gruff and mumbling way. She read it three times, and then she folded it small and kept it in her pocket.

One evening, Wren noticed Cassian sitting alone at a far table in the Hall, hunched over a heavy book with his chin in his hand. For once he did not look proud, only small and rather lonely beneath the great shelves, and she almost raised her hand to wave. Then he glanced up, saw her watching, snapped the book shut and strode away without a word.

Late that night, as Wren was leaving the Hall with a borrowed book under her arm, every book on every shelf stopped whispering at the very same moment. The silence was so sudden and so complete that it felt like a hand laid over her mouth, and a cold shiver ran slowly down her back. A few heartbeats later the whispers came back, one by one, but she stood there for a long time before she dared to move.

Wren hurried back toward the Sixth Gallery, taking the long stairs two at a time, and was relieved to find the lamps along its walls humming as sweetly as they always did. Halfway along the great curving hall, however, she slowed and then stopped, for something beneath her boots felt wrong, in a way that she could not at first put into words. She stood very still, as she had learned to do, and waited for the feeling to explain itself.

Wren knelt in the middle of the gallery and pressed her ear flat against the cold stone of the floor, ignoring the curious glance of an older student who hurried past. Beneath her she could hear the great, slow hum of the mountain, rich and deep as ever, except in one place, where a smooth and perfectly silent patch lay like a hole cut out with scissors. It was the most frightening sound she had ever heard, because it was no sound at all, and she had to fight an urge to run.

Once she had heard the silence, Wren could not stop hearing it, and the next morning, in Tuning class, she found the thin places everywhere she turned, like missing stitches in a long grey sock. Her pebble refused to answer her, and the more she worried, the worse her hum became, until she was staring at the stone with her teeth clenched. Across the room, Master Pike lifted his head and looked at her thoughtfully, as though he already guessed what was wrong.

When the others had gone, Pike asked Wren to stay behind, and he led her up a narrow stair to a small round office tucked under the roof of the gallery. It was crowded with lanterns of every shape and size, hung from the ceiling and stacked on shelves, all humming softly together like a choir at rest. He poured her a cup of hot, sweet tea without asking and told her to sit down.

Pike listened to everything that Wren told him without once interrupting, and when she had finished, he sighed, and put down his cup. He admitted that the Heartstone had been growing quiet for many months, that he had told only the Warden, and that a rumour of it might frighten the whole school into a worse kind of trouble. Then he asked Wren, very seriously, whether she would keep the secret a little while.

Pike gave her a small leather notebook and a stub of pencil, and told her to write down every silence she found, with the place, the day and the hour. Listening, he said, was not only a matter of hearing but a matter of paying careful and honest attention, and a worry that was written down was already half-tamed. Wren put the notebook in her pocket, next to her father's letter, and felt a little braver than before.

Keeping a secret from her friends turned out to be much harder than Wren had expected, especially with Priya, who could notice a change in the weather before it came. When Priya asked, with narrowed eyes, why Wren kept staring at the floor, she said that she was only homesick, and she disliked herself a little for the lie. Priya said nothing in reply, but she did not look as though she believed it.

In Stone class, Master Hale looked thinner and more tired than ever, with deep shadows under his eyes and a fresh scrape on one hand that he kept tucked into his sleeve. When the lamp above his desk flickered and dimmed, he stared at it in what seemed to be alarm, and then he excused himself abruptly and hurried from the room. The students whispered to one another, and Cassian stared hard at the empty doorway.

In a corridor between classes, Cassian stepped in front of Wren with his arms crossed and challenged her to a contest, to settle once and for all, he said, which of them was the best listener in their year. Wren told him politely that she did not want to compete, since listening was not a race, and then she walked around him and went on her way. That seemed to make him angrier than any insult could have done, and he glared after her all the way down the corridor.

One morning, the first snow of the winter came drifting down through the Skylight Shaft, a narrow chimney in the rock far above the great cavern, and it melted into silver mist long before it touched the bridges. Every student in the Academy was talking about Lantern Night, the midwinter festival, which was only three weeks away. For the first time in many days, Wren pushed her worries to the back of her mind and let herself feel excited.

In the weeks before midwinter, the whole school bustled with preparations, and every student spent long evenings in the workshop cave polishing a small brass lamp until it shone like a coin. On Lantern Night, Priya explained to the others, each of them would have to light that lamp with nothing but their own hum, in front of the whole Academy. Tobe, who had gone green around the mouth, looked as though he might be sick on the spot.

Night after night the three friends practised on the patchwork rug, humming at their brass lamps until their throats were sore, but not one of the wicks would catch. There were a few tiny sparks, however, and Wren noticed that each of them was a different colour, silver for Priya, gold for Tobe, and for herself a strange and brilliant blue. Priya said that her sparks looked like frost on a window and was clearly pleased about it.

On Lantern Night, the Hall of Lamps lay in total darkness, with its thousand lanterns hanging unlit from the high ceiling like sleeping bats. Snow drifted down through the Skylight Shaft in slow spirals and settled on the students' hair and shoulders, and nobody made a sound. Warden Marrow stood in the middle of the darkness with a single candle and said that every student would now lend the mountain a light of their own.

The students went up one at a time to a long stone table, and Priya was among the first, her chin held very high. She hummed one quick, clear note, and the wick of her lamp bloomed into a pale silver flame that sparkled like frost on a winter window. There was a pleased murmur from the hall, and then warm applause, and Priya turned round with a grin that stretched from ear to ear.

Tobe went up next, as pale as flour, and counted under his breath as he hummed, one, two, three, all the way to nine. His lamp glowed with a steady, warm golden flame that did not flicker even once, and he stared at it as though somebody else had made it. Wren and Priya cheered so loudly that Mistress Brook, nearby, had to hide a smile.

When her turn came, Wren stepped up to the stone table, shut her eyes, and did not hum at all at first, but simply listened to the little lamp as Pike had taught her. Then she lent it one clear note, and the wick blazed into a flame of such a bright and startling blue that the shadows leaped back from it across the whole hall. For a long moment, as the blue light danced on every face, nobody in the whole hall said anything at all.

Warden Marrow looked at the blue flame with her eyes wide, and then she turned her head slowly and looked at Master Pike, who had gone completely still. Wren could not tell whether his expression was gladness or fear, and she had a sinking feeling that it might be both. Then the Warden smiled, said that this was a fine lamp, and called the next name on her list.

Cassian stepped forward with his chin held high and hummed as loudly and forcefully as he could manage, but his lamp only sputtered, spat a few sparks and went out. He tried again, humming still harder, until the veins stood out on his neck, and the second time the wick did not even catch. A sympathetic silence settled over the hall, which was somehow far worse than any amount of laughter could have been.

Cassian whirled round, his face crimson, and accused Wren in front of the whole school of humming over him on purpose and spoiling his lamp. Warden Marrow replied, very calmly, that nobody could take another person's hum just by listening, and that it would be best if he went and sat down. It was an odd thing to say, Wren thought afterwards, and she wondered why her stomach felt so cold when she heard it.

When the last student had lit a lamp, the Warden announced that a quarrel on Lantern Night was no way to begin a winter. Cassian and Wren would therefore clean the soot from the lamp tunnels together every evening for a week, she said, and Cassian looked at Wren with a horror that Wren returned exactly. Behind them, Priya tried to hide a laugh in her sleeve and failed completely.

The lamp tunnels ran behind every gallery of the Academy, low and narrow and smelling of old smoke, and the lamps inside them were black with years of soot. On the first evening, Wren and Cassian scrubbed side by side with their buckets between them, and in a silence so cold that she half expected frost to form on the cloths. Cassian held his rag between two fingers, at arm's length, as though it might bite him at any moment.

By the second evening, Cassian could not keep quiet any longer, and he announced that Wren obviously thought she was special because of her stupid blue lamp. Wren replied hotly that she did not think anything of the kind, that she had only listened to the lamp before she hummed, and that this was hardly a crime. They went on in fierce whispers that bounced back and forth along the tunnel until they were both red in the face.

Old Ibb appeared at the mouth of the tunnel with a pot of steaming tea and two chipped cups, and he poured them each a cupful without a word of comment on their red faces. Lamp soot, he remarked, was the breath of the mountain, and these old tunnels had long memories and very little patience with quarrelling. Then he winked at Wren, tapped his broom against the wall twice, and shuffled away into the shadows.

On the third evening, tired of the silence, Wren showed Cassian how to rest his hand on a lamp and listen to it before he touched it with the cloth. He tried it very reluctantly, with his jaw set, but the soot lifted from the glass much more easily than before, and he looked at the clean surface with a sort of grudging astonishment. Neither of them said anything, but the cold between them had thawed by a degree.

On the fifth evening, as they scrubbed their way along a stretch of the tunnel behind the Fifth Gallery, Wren stopped and held up her hand. Every lamp in that section was lit, yet not one of them hummed, as if the song had been drawn out of the flames and only the glow left behind. The light itself looked different, flat and thin and strangely lifeless, like a painted sun.

To Wren's astonishment, Cassian laid his hand on one of the silent lamps, frowned, and slowly went pale in the dim light. He admitted in a low voice that he could feel it as well, and that it did not seem to him like an ordinary silence, but like something that had been taken on purpose. It was the first time that he had ever said something to her without a hint of scorn.

They agreed, crouching close together in the dim tunnel, that it would be wise to say nothing until they understood more about what they had found. Cassian muttered, almost to himself, that his uncle Corvin had scarcely slept since the autumn and wandered the galleries at night, and that he had not been able to find out why. Wren said nothing about Pike's secret, which she had promised to keep, but she felt a flicker of unease.

That night, in the small hours, the lamps of the Fifth Gallery failed one by one, like candles in a draught, and even the glowing moss on the walls faded to black. The students woke in a cold and absolute darkness, with their breath showing in the air, and somewhere along the hall a small child began to cry. It was the first time in a thousand years, someone whispered, that the lights had gone out.

Warden Marrow hurried into the gallery with a single candle, and she did not scold or explain or tell anybody not to be silly. Instead she began to sing, in her low, clear, bell-like voice, a slow song without words that seemed to wrap itself around the huddled children like a blanket. One by one, the whimpering stopped, and the dark seemed a little less hostile.

Afterwards, when the lamps had flickered dimly back to life, Wren pulled Priya and Tobe aside and told them everything about the silences and the notebook, and said that she was sorry for the lie. Priya gave her a hard look, and then a hug, and said that investigating was the only sensible thing to do, and Tobe agreed. Cassian, who had been standing nearby in the shadows, cleared his throat and asked, stiffly, whether he might join them.

In a quiet corner of the Hall of Held Breath, the four friends spread a large map of the Academy across the floor and weighed its corners down with heavy books. Tobe, who loved nothing better than a problem with numbers in it, produced a stub of chalk and marked every silence from Wren's notebook with a neat little cross. A nearby book whispered a rude comment about the chalk, and Priya whispered something just as rude back.

When every cross had been marked, a pattern appeared that nobody had expected, for the silences were not scattered at random across the Academy. They ran in a crooked line, gallery by gallery and stair by stair, steadily downward, and the line ended at the one place that every student had been warned against. Tobe tapped the final cross with his chalk and said, very quietly, that it was the Ninth Stair.

Priya had an idea, and one night she tested it by humming a thin line of frost across the floor of the Fifth Gallery, as straight as a ruler. The frost ran smoothly along the stone until it reached one of the silent patches, and there it stopped dead, as though it had struck an invisible wall. She tried again in three more places and, each time, the frost refused to cross, which told them exactly where the edges were.

Cassian, to everyone's surprise, turned out to be extremely useful, for his strong and heavy hum could sense the edges of a silence like a hand pressing on a bruise. He crouched on the floor night after night with his jaw set and his eyes closed, calling out distances to Tobe, who wrote them down. Slowly, without anybody saying so, the three friends began to treat him as one of their own.

They decided at last to watch the Fifth Gallery at night, in the hope of seeing whoever, or whatever, was making the silences. Wrapped in blankets and fortified by Tobe's endless supply of bread, they took turns to stay awake while the cold crept around their ankles and the moss dimmed overhead. Nothing happened on the first night, or the second, or the third, and Priya began to grumble.

On the fourth night, a little after midnight, a cloaked figure came walking soundlessly along the gallery with a glass jar cradled in both hands, keeping close to the wall. It stopped beside a lamp, lifted the jar, and held it close to the flame as a person might hold a cup under a spring. The four friends, flattened against the wall in the dark, did not dare to breathe or even to blink.

A thread of pale silver light curled out of the flame and into the mouth of the jar, and as it flowed, the lamp's hum faded slowly away to nothing. The figure screwed a lid onto the glass, with the care of a person closing a letter, and the whole gallery seemed to grow colder. Wren felt her stomach twist, for it was exactly as if she had watched someone steal the voice of a sleeping child, quietly and without any apology.

Priya's foot slipped on a patch of her own frost, and she gasped aloud before she could stop herself. The cloaked figure whipped around, hesitated for a single heartbeat, and then ran away into the darkness with the jar held tightly against its chest. The four friends scrambled to their feet and, without anybody giving the order, ran after it.

The chase took them through winding galleries, down narrow stairs and across swaying footbridges, with Tobe counting every turn under his breath so that they could find their way back. Cassian shouted at the figure to stop in his most commanding voice, but it only ran faster, and its cloak billowed out behind it like a dark wing. Wren's lungs burned, and the hum of her own heartbeat drowned out everything else.

At the end of a long, dead-ended gallery, the figure ran straight at a blank stone wall and simply vanished into it, like a swimmer diving into a pool. By the time the four friends staggered up, panting, there was nothing before them but the plain grey stone, which hummed faintly and did not look as though it had ever opened. On the floor in front of it, however, lay a single folded page, which must have fallen from the figure's cloak.

Wren unfolded the page with great care in the light of Tobe's small lantern, while the others pressed close around her. It showed a careful drawing in black ink of a great crystal at the bottom of a spiral stair, with doors, arches and numbers scattered all around it, and a few lines of neat writing below. Nobody spoke, and the only sound in the little circle of light was the quick, nervous sound of their breathing.

Beneath the drawing, in a small and careful hand, were written the words that when the mountain was quiet, she would wake. Cassian leaned over Wren's shoulder to read them, stiffened as though he had been struck, and went as pale as milk in the lantern light. When Priya asked him what was wrong, he did not answer her at all.

Cassian took the page from Wren's fingers, studied the writing for a long moment with his lips pressed together, and then turned and walked quickly away into the dark without saying a single word. The others pressed after him with questions, but he only shook his head and kept going. That night Wren lay awake staring at the glowing moss and wondering what Cassian could possibly know.

The next evening, Wren found Cassian sitting all by himself on a quiet stone stair in a forgotten corner of the Academy, with a small lamp at his side and the folded page resting on his knee. She did not say anything clever, for she had learned that Pike's first rule applied to people as well as stones, but simply sat down beside him and listened to the silence. After a long while, Cassian cleared his throat and began to speak in a low voice.

Cassian told her, in a flat and careful voice, that the handwriting on the page belonged to his uncle, Master Corvin Hale. He knew it better than his own, he said, because his uncle had written to him every month since he was six years old, in exactly the same neat and patient hand, long before Cassian came to the Academy. Wren said that she was sorry, and meant it, and she did not try to fill the quiet that followed.

Cassian explained, in fits and starts, that his parents were mapmakers who were always travelling in far countries, and that he had spent most of his summers at the Academy with his uncle. Master Hale had once been warm and funny, he said, and had taught him chess and how to whistle through a blade of grass. Over the last few years, however, something in him had gone out, like a lamp running dry, and it occurred to Wren that the hammer in Cassian's hum might simply be loneliness.

Wren told him gently that nobody could be blamed until they had found out the truth, and that the page might mean something quite different from what it seemed. Cassian nodded slowly, and asked her in a very small voice not to tell the teachers just yet, and Wren promised that she would say nothing until they knew a great deal more. Then they walked back to the Sixth Gallery together, in a long silence that was not at all unfriendly, and Wren found that she no longer minded his company.

Back in the round room, Cassian told Priya and Tobe what he had told Wren, stumbling over the words, and for once neither of them made a joke or looked at him strangely. Tobe thought for a long minute, with his round face screwed up, and then suggested that they should ask Ibb, who had been at the Academy longer than anybody could remember and who knew every old story in the mountain. Priya said that it was the first sensible thing anyone had said all week.

In his warm stable cave, with the two mules munching hay in the corner, Ibb poked the fire and hung a kettle over it. He settled the four children on a row of upturned buckets as though he had been expecting them, and he said nothing for a long time. At last, in his dry, slow voice, he began to tell them about a girl named Elin Hale, while Cassian sat very still with his hands gripped between his knees.

Thirty years ago, Ibb said, Master Hale had a daughter called Elin, who was the finest listener that the Academy had ever seen. One night, at the age of fifteen, she went alone below the Ninth Stair to hear the Heartstone sing, and she was never seen again, though some people said that her echo still lingered in the stone. After that, he told them quietly, Master Hale had never truly smiled, and the Ninth Stair had been forbidden to every student.

Walking back from Ibb's cave, the four friends were silent for a long while, until Tobe wondered aloud who the she in the page might be. Cassian answered in a very quiet voice that it must be Elin, and that his uncle must hope that, if the mountain fell silent enough, her echo would wake. Nobody said what they were all thinking, which was that grief can make a good man do a very strange thing.

Winter deepened over the mountain, and more lamps lost their hum in more distant galleries, though the cloaked figure never returned to the Fifth. Every few days there was a new cut, and every new cut meant a new chalk cross on Tobe's map, while the friends drank hot soup in the dining hall and pretended, as best they could, that everything was normal. Wren noticed that Master Hale ate almost nothing at all, and that he watched the door of the hall as though he were waiting for someone.

One cold morning, Pike announced to the class that the spring test of the first year would be the Long Note, which was the oldest test at the Academy and the one that most students dreaded. Each of them would have to hold a single, steady hum, without a break, for one whole hour, and he did not expect any of them to manage it for a very long time. A long groan went round the Quiet Room, and Tobe quietly began to count the minutes in an hour.

In the first attempts, most of the students lasted only a few minutes before their hum wobbled, cracked and stopped, and the Quiet Room filled with embarrassed coughs. Priya sneezed at the third minute and declared that her nose was the problem, while Tobe, who counted silently behind his hum, lasted the longest of them all. Wren, for her part, let her mind wander to her father's lane and lost the note at ten minutes.

Cassian attacked the Long Note with all of his strength, as though it were an enemy to be beaten, and his hum cracked in half after four minutes. Pike told him gently that this test was not about strength at all, but about patience, and that a hum which would last an hour must bend like grass in a wind rather than stand like a wall. Cassian looked at him as if he had been told to walk on water.

Wren discovered a trick of her own, which was to stop trying and to think instead of the slow, steady breathing of her father's lamp in the lane at home. The hum seemed to flow out of her without any effort at all, as easy as a stream running down a hill, and she held it for twenty whole minutes before her throat grew tired. When she opened her eyes, Pike was watching her with a small, approving nod.

In the lamp tunnels where they had once scrubbed side by side, Wren patiently helped Cassian to practise a softer, rounder hum, sitting beside him night after night and saying very little. After many failures, he held a note for ten whole minutes, and when he opened his eyes they were shining with something that might have been tears. He said, gruffly, that it was a good deal harder than being a hammer.

In Echo class, Mistress Brook showed Tobe how to turn his counting into one long, unbroken song, rising and falling like a tide. He lost himself entirely in the numbers, and the cave sang them back to him in a golden shimmer, and he held the note for half an hour without even noticing that time had passed. Mistress Brook wiped her eyes and said that she had never heard anything like it in twenty years.

The first thaw came at last, and the whole mountain filled with the sound of dripping water, so that the hum of the stone became a bright, trickling song. A letter arrived from Alder, written in his careful hand, and folded inside it was a pressed snowdrop from the lane at Hollin Ford, a little squashed but still faintly white. Wren set it carefully inside the cover of her notebook, next to the map of silences.

That night the four friends sat in a circle on the patchwork rug with their hands joined and the little stove ticking beside them. They promised one another that every one of them would pass the Long Note, and that they would not stop until they had found out the truth about the silences. Priya, who was never very good at serious moments, ruined it by laughing, and soon they were all laughing together.

In spring the first-year students were taken on a special trip to the Singing Falls, an underground waterfall far below the galleries, which Wren had heard about from older students in hushed and excited voices. Master Hale and Mistress Brook led the way, with Hale walking a little apart from the rest, and every student carried a small lantern that swung and flickered as they walked. Tobe counted the steps again, as he always did, and reached six hundred and four before the roaring drowned him out.

The tunnel was long and cold and damp, winding steadily downward through the rock, and the walls glistened in the lantern light like the inside of a shell. A distant roaring grew louder with every step they took, until it seemed to shake the very stones beneath their boots and to rattle the glass of their lanterns. Priya grabbed Wren's hand in the dark without seeming to notice that she had done so, and Wren did not let go.

They stepped out together onto a wide stone ledge, and there before them were the Singing Falls, a colossal waterfall that poured out of a crack high in the cavern roof and plunged into a dark and bottomless lake. The water did not simply roar as any other waterfall would have done, but sang, in a hundred different voices, high and low, mingling and parting, so that the whole cave seemed to be full of an invisible choir. Wren's eyes filled with tears, and she could not have said, for all the gold in the world, exactly why.

Mistress Brook raised her voice above the roar to tell the class that water remembered every song that had ever fallen into it, whether it was sung by a student or by a queen. One by one, each student sent a note toward the falls, and the water caught it, carried it away and wove it into the choir, so that for a moment their own small voices were part of something enormous. Even Cassian, at the end of the row, smiled openly, for the first time that anybody had seen, and nobody teased him.

Master Hale did not sing with the others, but stood apart at the very edge of the ledge, staring down into the dark lake with a lost expression. His lips moved slightly, as though he were speaking to someone in the water, and Cassian, a few steps away, never took his eyes from his uncle's face. Wren turned away, feeling that she had seen something that she was not meant to see.

When the others had finished, Wren stayed behind to listen to the great song of the Falls on her own, and her heart sank. Somewhere in the middle of that enormous choir, there was a thin gap, narrow as a knife-cut and perfectly silent, exactly like the silences in the lamps. The mountain was losing its song even here, in the one place where its voice had always seemed the strongest and the most free.

Wren whispered the news to her friends behind a screen of drifting spray, where no teacher could possibly overhear them above the thunder of the water. Tobe frowned and gazed up at the dark roof of the cavern, as though he were trying to remember something important, and then he began very slowly to move his lips. Priya asked him what he was doing, and he asked her to be quiet for a moment.

Tobe pulled out Wren's notebook, smoothed it flat on his knee, and counted the dates on his fingers, whispering numbers to himself. After a long minute he looked up with an expression of astonishment, and said that every silence they had found had come on a ninth night, counting from the first, without a single exception. Nobody, including Wren, who had written the dates down herself, had ever thought to count the nights between them.

Tobe counted forward on his fingers once more, checked it twice, and announced that the next ninth night would fall on Thursday, which was only three days away. The friends looked at one another with their hearts beating fast, because for the first time they knew exactly where and when to look. Cassian whispered that he did not want to be right about his uncle, and then he fell silent.

Back at the Academy, the four friends hurried to Master Pike and laid out everything they had discovered, from the lamps and the jar to Tobe's count of the nights, although Cassian kept the page in his pocket. Pike listened gravely and said that the Warden would be away on the mountain until Friday, and that until then they must do nothing but watch from the Eighth Gallery. If they saw anyone near the Ninth Stair, they were to ring the small brass bell that he gave them, and he would come at once.

On Wednesday night, the four friends made their plan on the patchwork rug with great seriousness, as if they were generals about to go to war. Priya would bring the warm cloaks, Tobe would bring the bread, and Wren would carry the little brass bell, while Cassian asked in a small voice what would happen if he had been wrong about his uncle. Nobody could answer him, but Wren held out her hand and he took it.

Thursday dragged by with agonising slowness, and Master Hale taught Stone class that afternoon more gently than he had done in many weeks, as though something heavy had been lifted from his shoulders. As the students filed out, he laid a hand on Cassian's shoulder and told him, very quietly, to take good care of himself, and Cassian went white and could not speak. Wren, standing just behind him in the doorway, felt the hair rise on the back of her neck.

When evening came, the four friends crept up to the Eighth Gallery, a high, narrow stone balcony that looked out over the great stair leading down to the lower levels of the Academy. They crouched behind its carved balustrade, wrapped in Priya's cloaks, with the brass bell in Wren's pocket and the lamps all around them burning low. Below them, the long stair curved away into a darkness that seemed almost to breathe, slowly and patiently, like a sleeping animal.

They waited for many long hours, sharing Tobe's bread and whispering very little, while the cold seeped slowly into their bones. Priya's nervous frost crept over the stone rail in feathery patterns, Tobe counted each hour under his breath, and Wren listened to the mountain's hum, which had worn so thin that it trembled like a spider's thread. She had never in her life wished so strongly that something would hold, and she kept her fingers crossed inside her cloak.

At midnight, a deep bell tolled somewhere in the depths of the Academy, and its great note rolled slowly outward across the cavern until it died among the bridges. The four friends went absolutely still, for it was the ninth night, and even Tobe forgot to count. In the silence that followed, Wren thought that she could hear her own pulse hammering in her ears like a small drum.

A figure in a long, dark cloak came slowly up the great stair from the lower levels, carrying a basket that clinked softly with glass at every step. It carried no light of its own and kept close to the wall, in the manner of someone who has walked that path in the dark many times before. The four friends did not dare to breathe or move as it drew slowly nearer to the foot of the gallery.

As the figure passed beneath a lamp, its hood slipped back, and the light fell across a thin, tired, grey-haired face that all four of them knew. It was Master Hale, and Cassian whispered the word uncle so quietly that only Wren heard it, and she reached out and gripped his arm hard. For a moment he swayed where he stood, and then he steadied himself against the cold stone of the balustrade.

Hale stopped beside a lamp, lifted an empty jar with trembling hands, and drew the lamp's hum into it, thread by shining thread, as the others watched from above. They could hear him murmuring, very softly, as though he were talking to a child, that it would not be long now and that soon, soon, he would see Elin again. The lamp fell silent, and the dark seemed to deepen around his stooped shoulders, and Wren heard the mountain's hum waver faintly.

Cassian took the bell from Wren's hand and stared at it for a long, painful moment, torn between his love for his uncle and the promise they had made to Pike. Then, with a face as white as paper, he lifted it and rang it, and its clear, bright note rang out across the cavern and echoed from gallery to gallery. He said afterwards that it was the hardest thing he had ever done, and the others never doubted it for a moment.

Below them, Hale froze at the sound with his face turned up in alarm, and for a moment he seemed to look straight at the four small faces peering through the balustrade. Then he snatched up his basket and hurried away down the great stair toward the Ninth, and the darkness quickly swallowed the sound of his footsteps. Wren knew in that instant that if they stayed where they were, he would be gone, and with him the truth.

At the head of the Ninth Stair, an old rusty chain hung across the opening, with a small, faded sign beside it that said only that the way was closed. The four friends stopped short, panting, and every one of them remembered the second rule that the Warden had given them on their very first day. Below them, in the gloom, the sound of Hale's footsteps was growing steadily fainter, and nobody had yet said what they should do.

Wren shut her eyes and did what she had been taught to do, which was to listen first, before she did anything else. The mountain's hum was thin and urgent, and it seemed to be drawing her downward, as if it needed somebody to come, and the chain no longer felt to her like an order but like a thread of rust.
