She opened her eyes and told the others, in a voice that was steadier than she felt, that they had to follow him.

One by one, the four friends climbed over the chain and set their feet on the first of the forbidden steps, which were cold and slightly damp. Tobe was trembling from head to foot, but he began to count the steps in a whisper, and the numbers seemed to steady all four of them like a rope. Priya lifted her lantern high, Cassian took the lead without being asked, and then the four of them went down into the dark together.

The stair wound downward in a tight spiral, round and round, and the glowing moss on the walls slowly changed from green to a deep and cloudy blue. With every turn the hum of the mountain grew deeper and slower, until it seemed to Wren to be the beat of an enormous heart, and she found that her own pulse was falling into step with it. Nobody spoke, and even the sound of their footsteps seemed to be swallowed up by the deep, dark walls on either side.

Lower down, the steps grew wet and treacherous, shining with a thin film of water, and Cassian slipped and nearly pitched headlong into the dark. Priya hummed one quick, bright note and scattered a fine layer of frost on every step ahead of them, which gripped their boots like sand and made the descent far safer. She pretended, afterwards, that it had been nothing at all, though she looked quietly proud of herself all the way down.

Halfway down, the light of Wren's lantern fell on some words scratched into the stone wall, very small and a little crooked, as though by a child with a sharp pebble. They said, Elin Hale was here, aged fifteen, and under them was a tiny drawing of a lamp. Cassian stared at the writing without making a sound, and then he reached out and laid his hand flat over it.

Tobe counted out loud as he always did, and the echo of his voice came back from below much sooner than before, which meant, as Mistress Brook had taught them, that the floor of the stair was close. At the same moment Wren held up her hand for silence, for she had heard the footsteps below them stop, and the only sound was a faint clinking of glass. Slowly, holding their breath, they crept down the last few turns of the stair on tiptoe.

At the bottom of the stair stood a great arched door of black stone, traced all over with fine silver lines that glimmered like frost in the lantern light. Master Hale was standing before it with his back toward them and his basket of jars at his feet, as still as a statue, listening to something that none of them could hear. Then, without turning round, he spoke to them in a quiet and weary voice.

Hale turned slowly, and he was not angry at all, only unspeakably tired, like a man who has carried a heavy load for thirty years. He told the children, in a low and gentle voice, that the Heartstone's song was so loud and old that it drowned his daughter's echo. If the mountain grew quiet enough, he had hoped, she might wake and speak to him once more, and he had only meant to borrow the hum for a little while.

Hale laid his palm against the black door, and the silver lines flared suddenly into light, running across the stone like water finding its way down a hillside. Slowly and without a sound the great door swung open, and a pale, trembling glow spilled out over the four children's faces and made their shadows long behind them. It was the glow of the Heartstone, the heart of the whole mountain, and it was much fainter than any of them had expected.

Behind the door lay the Hollow, a vast domed chamber carved out of the living rock, so wide that the far wall was lost in shadow. In the very middle of it stood the Heartstone, a crystal as big as a farmhouse, and its pale light rose and fell and flickered like a candle in a draught. The four children stood in the doorway, and none of them could think of a single thing to say.

Hale walked slowly across the smooth black floor and set his basket down at the foot of the great crystal, with the tenderness of a man putting down a sleeping child. The jars inside it began to glow and whisper faintly, as though they knew where they were and were eager to go home. Wren could feel their small, stolen songs tugging at her chest like homesick children.

Wren crossed the floor, step by careful step, and laid her ear flat against the cool, smooth surface of the Heartstone, feeling the tiny trembling of it against her cheek. Inside the crystal, a pale light moved slowly round and round, like a fish in a deep and endless pool, and with it moved a hum so large and so low that she felt it in her teeth. She closed her eyes and listened with every single part of herself, exactly as Pike had taught her to do.

Slowly, as the great hum rolled through her, Wren understood what she was hearing. The song travelled in an enormous circle, from the Heartstone to every lamp and wall and stair in the Academy, and then home again to the crystal. Each of the jars that Hale had filled had cut a little more out of that circle, she realised, and the only way to heal it was to carry the stolen hum home.

Wren turned from the crystal and told Hale as gently as she could what she had heard, and how the missing hum was breaking the circle. He shook his head slowly, as if each word were a small blow, and said that he had only wanted to borrow a little, and that he had never meant to keep it for ever. His voice shook, and Wren saw that he was a man who had not been listened to for a very long time.

Wren leaned against the crystal once more and listened deeper than she had ever listened in her life, past the great hum and past the little songs of the jars. There, in a stillness so complete that it rang, she heard a girl's voice, very small and very far away, which was no more than an echo, saying clearly and patiently that the song must go home. A faint shape, like a figure made of light, shimmered for a heartbeat in the heart of the stone.

Wren turned to Hale and told him, with trembling lips, exactly what she had heard, repeating the words as carefully as she could, because she knew they were the most precious ones that he would ever be given. For a long time he stood like a statue in the shimmering light, and his face went through a hundred changes without his speaking a word. Then he put both hands over his eyes, and his shoulders began very slowly to shake.

Hale sank to his knees in front of the Heartstone and wept as though thirty years of tears had been waiting for their turn. Cassian knelt beside him and took his hand, and said in a steady and surprisingly gentle voice that it was time to give back what he had borrowed, as the third rule taught. Hale looked at his nephew as if he were seeing him for the first time in years.

With shaking fingers, Hale unscrewed the jars one after another and laid the lids carefully on the floor. The stolen hum rose from each one in a bright thread of silver light, and the threads flowed like little rivers across the black stone toward the Heartstone, merging as they went into one great, shining stream. The crystal gave a deep sigh, and its glow trembled and began slowly to rise.

Wren, Priya, Tobe and Cassian stood together around the glowing crystal and each lent it their own hum, silver and gold and blue and strong, until the Hollow rang like a bell. Hale lifted his head, wiped his face with his sleeve, and added his deep, cracked voice to theirs, and together the five of them sang the song of the mountain back to its heart. It was the most beautiful sound that Wren had ever heard, and she knew that it was not yet finished.

The ringing of the bell had woken the whole Academy, and Master Pike came running down the Ninth Stair with Warden Marrow, who had returned early from the mountain, and a long stream of teachers and students pouring behind them. Lanterns bobbed and swayed all the way up the spiral, and the sound of many feet rolled down like thunder. At the great door of the Hollow, with their lanterns still swinging, they all came to a sudden halt.

At the threshold of the Hollow they stopped in astonishment, for the sight that met them was like nothing any of them had seen before. Four children and a grey-haired teacher stood around the Heartstone in a ring, with threads of silver light flowing toward the crystal, and the whole chamber was ringing with a song. Warden Marrow raised her hand, and every voice behind her fell silent at once.

One by one, the newcomers understood what they were hearing, and they began to sing. Pike's deep voice came in first, then Mistress Brook's, ringing and sweet, then Ibb's dry old rasp, and after them every teacher and student in the Academy, until the whole Hollow was full of voices. Even the Warden, after a long moment, closed her eyes and added her bell-like voice to the rest.

The song grew louder and fuller with every breath, until it seemed to shake the very stone of the chamber and make the lanterns tremble in the students' hands. The Heartstone began to blaze, and its light turned from pale grey to warm gold to a dazzling white that made everyone shield their eyes. Wren stood in the middle of it all, humming with her whole heart, and felt the mountain hum back.

In the heart of the blazing crystal, a shape began to rise like mist from a still lake at dawn. It was a girl of fifteen made of soft golden light, with plaits down her back and a smile on her face, and everyone in the Hollow knew without being told that it was Elin's echo. Nobody dared to breathe or move, for fear that the lovely shape might fade away before they had understood it.

Elin's echo looked at her father with kind eyes, and her voice, when it came, was as warm and clear as a spring morning. She told him that she had never been lost, only listening, and that she was thankful beyond words that he had loved her so well and waited so long. Then she told him that it was time to put down the weight he had been carrying.

Hale whispered her name, and she smiled at him, and then at Cassian, who was still holding his uncle's hand with all his strength. She asked her father, very gently, to teach the song to others, as he had once taught it to her, so that no listener would ever have to be lonely in the dark. Hale nodded, though tears ran freely down his cheeks, and he said that he would.

Elin's echo turned to the others, thanked them one by one with a small bow, and then slowly faded back into the golden light of the Heartstone. She went like the last note of a song, so softly and so gradually that nobody could have said exactly when she was gone, and the Hollow was filled with a deep and holy peace. Hale smiled, for the first time in thirty years, and the smile reached all the way to his tired grey eyes.

The circle had closed, and the great hum of the Heartstone was whole again, deep and steady and rich with every song that had been borrowed and brought home. Wren laid her palm against the crystal, and she could feel the mountain's gratitude flowing up her arm like warm water, wordless and enormous. She wanted to laugh and cry at once, and she found that she was doing both.

Across the whole Academy the lamps flared up again at the very same moment, from the lowest tunnel to the highest gallery, and every bridge and tower sprang into golden light. The moss glowed green on every wall, the chill lifted from every hall and stair, and in the Sixth Gallery, where the younger students had been left behind, a great cheer went up. The children at the rail were certain that the mountain itself was singing, and for once nobody tried to argue.

The whole company climbed the Ninth Stair together, tired and happy and humming softly, with Master Hale walking slowly between Cassian and Pike. At the top, beside the rusty chain, Ibb was waiting with his broom under one arm and an enormous pot of tea in his hand. He remarked, without a trace of surprise, that it had taken them long enough, and nobody could ever say how he had known.

In her lamplit study, Master Hale stood before Warden Marrow with his head bowed and told her the whole truth, from the first jar to the last, leaving nothing out and making no excuses for himself. The four children stood beside him and added their own part, including the chain they had climbed over and the rule that they had broken, because Wren said that it would be wrong to leave it out. The Warden listened to everything in silence, without once interrupting, and her face gave nothing away until the very end.

To everyone's surprise, Warden Marrow did not send Master Hale away, as many students had whispered she would. Instead she gave him the care of the Heartstone, saying that nobody in the Academy understood its loneliness better than he did. She told the children that their courage had been great, but that a rule was never a thing to be broken lightly, and the four of them nodded and tried very hard to look sorry.

At breakfast, Warden Marrow stood up before the whole school and announced a new tradition, which would be added to the Academy's old customs from that day forward. Every spring, she said, the entire school would gather in the great hall and sing to the mountain, so that the Academy might always give back some part of what it was given. She called it Giving Back, and it was the third rule, made visible for all to see.

At the first Giving Back, the whole school gathered beneath the thousand lamps of the great hall and sang together, small children and tall teachers side by side, in a single, rolling, golden voice. The lamps hummed along with them, the Falls sent up their own deep note from far below, and the mountain seemed to answer from every stone and every wall. Wren thought that her father would have liked to hear it more than anything in the world.

A few days afterward, Cassian found Wren eating bread by herself on one of the high bridges, and with great effort he apologised for his first-day sneer and for the unkind things that followed it. He thanked her for what she had done for his uncle, and then, for the first time, he laughed in a way that was warm and open. From that afternoon on, the four of them, Wren, Priya, Tobe and Cassian, were rarely apart.

Master Hale began to smile again, slowly and a little shyly, like someone trying out a half-forgotten skill, and in the evenings he played chess with Cassian beside the Heartstone in its warm and steady glow. His Stone lessons changed as well, filled with stories and jokes and long, patient pauses, and the students said that his voice had found its colour at last. Cassian's hum, too, grew a little gentler every week, and the harshness in it slowly wore away like a rough edge on a river stone.

In the weeks that remained before the test, the four friends were never apart, and the Academy seemed to belong to them alone. Tobe drew a vast and beautiful map of every lamp in the Academy, with a number for each one. Priya froze the surface of a small pool beside the Falls so that all four of them could slide across it, shrieking with laughter, and Wren thought that she had never been so happy in her whole life.

On the day of the Long Note, the first-year students sat in rows in the Quiet Room, nervous and silent, with their hands resting on their knees and their eyes already closed. Pike reminded them, in his calm and gentle voice, that the hour was not a race to be won but a gift of patience that each of them was giving to the mountain. Then he rang a small silver bell, and the long hour began in a deep and listening silence.

Wren thought of her father's lamp in the village lane, slow and steady and patient, and the hum flowed out of her as easily as breathing. Minute after minute, the whole hour went by without her feeling the time pass, and when the last grain of sand finally ran through the glass, she was still humming softly and had to be told to stop. Pike's eyes were shining as he nodded to her, and the hall was silent with wonder.

Priya, Tobe and Cassian all passed the Long Note as well, Priya declaring proudly that her nose had behaved itself for the entire hour, and Cassian's soft, steady hum was praised by Pike in front of the whole class. That night the school held a farewell feast at long tables beneath the thousand lamps of the great hall. There were roast chestnuts, honey cakes and a mountain of bread, which Tobe inspected with professional interest.

On the last evening, standing on a stone bridge above the glowing city, Priya tied a blue ribbon around Wren's wrist, and Tobe handed her a lopsided loaf that he had baked himself in the Academy's kitchens. They promised to meet again in the autumn, and none of the three of them managed to say goodbye without crying a little. Priya said that she was not crying and that it was only the frost.

In the stable cave, Wren said goodbye to Ibb and to Dumpling, who was eating a carrot with an air of great dignity and did not look up. Ibb leaned on his broom and told her, with a twinkle, that giving back was the whole of it, and that all the rest was only details. Then he pulled a clean handkerchief out of his sleeve and blew his nose into it with a trumpeting noise.

Cassian handed Wren a small folded map of the Academy that he had drawn himself, with every gallery and bridge and stair named in neat, careful writing, and the Sixth Gallery marked with a tiny star. He told her, rather shyly, that he would spend the summer with his uncle, who wished to thank her again for listening when nobody else had. He said that he looked forward to seeing her in the autumn more than he could say.

At the Great Door, on the morning she left, Master Pike gave Wren a small lantern of her own, made of brass and glass and no heavier than a loaf of bread. It burned without oil, as his did, and its hum was soft and clear and seemed to fit hers like a glove. He told her that a listener should always carry a little light that she has made herself.

Wren hummed one quiet note at the Great Door, and it swung open at once, as if it were sorry to see her go and already glad that she would be back. Dumpling plodded out into the bright spring sunshine with her round ears flicking, and the whole wide valley opened below them in a haze of green. Wren turned in the saddle and waved, and the carved lamps on the door glowed for a moment in reply.

With Master Pike beside her, Wren rode down the mountain for three days, through the bare grey slopes, the pine woods and the green fields beyond. The mountain's deep hum grew fainter behind her with every mile, but she never lost it entirely, and ahead of her she began to hear, very faintly, the small bright songs of the lamps of home. Pike turned back at the last crossroads, bowing low and wishing her a good summer, and Wren rode the last few miles alone.

At the village gate Dill Hobbs stood awkwardly with his cap in his hands, red to the ears, and mumbled a hello. He asked her, in a rush, what the mountain was like, and when Wren told him about the Door, the moss and the cavern full of lamps, he listened with his mouth hanging open and did not laugh once. At the end he asked, very quietly and without any mockery at all, whether the lamps really did hum.

Wren ran down the lane as fast as her boots would carry her and threw her arms around her father, who dropped his taper with a laugh that was half a sob. She showed him the lantern that Pike had given her, and the stone, and Cassian's map, while he said that he had been quite certain all spring that the lamps in the lane were missing her. Then he held her at arm's length, looked at her for a long moment, and said that she had grown at least a foot.

As the first stars came out over Hollin Ford, Wren and her father lit the first lamp of the evening together, as they had so many times before. Inside the flame, beneath its crackle and its small bright song, she heard the faint, deep hum of the mountain, and she knew that it had followed her home. She smiled, pressed her ear against the warm glass, and listened, for the Academy would be waiting for her again in the autumn.
